Decomposition into BCNF: Decompose along the violating dependency $Instructor \rightarrow Course$: $R_1(Instructor, Course)$ with $F_1 = \{Instructor \rightarrow Course\}$. Candidate key: $Instructor$. (In BCNF) $R_2(Student, Instructor)$ with Candidate key: $(Student, Instructor)$. (In BCNF) 4. Dependency Preservation: $F_1 \cup F_2$ contains $Instructor \rightarrow Course$, but the original dependency $Student, Course \rightarrow Instructor$ cannot be checked without joining $R_1$ and $R_2$. The BCNF decomposition is Lossless, but DOES NOT preserve the functional dependency $Student, Course \rightarrow Instructor$.

title: Consider the relation Course_Offering(Course_ID, Semester, Instructor, Room, Instructor_Dept) with the functional dependencies {Course_ID, Semester -> Instructor, Room; Instructor -> Instructor_Dept}. Find the candidate key, analyse which of 2NF, 3NF and BCNF the relation satisfies, decompose it into 3NF, and verify that the decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving.
chunks: 1. Candidate Key Determination: Compute closure of $(Course\_ID, Semester)$: $(Course\_ID, Semester)^+ = \{Course\_ID, Semester, Instructor, Room, Instructor\_Dept\}$ Unique Candidate Key: (Course_ID, Semester) . Prime attributes: Course_ID , Semester . Non-prime: Instructor , Room , Instructor_Dept . 2. Normal Form Analysis: 2NF: Both dependencies have LHS as either the full key ( Course_ID, Semester ) or a non-prime attribute ( Instructor ). No non-prime depends on a proper subset of the key. Hence, it satisfies 2NF . 3NF: In $Instructor \rightarrow Instructor\_Dept$, $Instructor$ is not a super key and $Instructor\_Dept$ is not prime. This is a transitive dependency . Hence, it violates 3NF . 3. Decomposition into 3NF: $R_1(Instructor, Instructor\_Dept)$ with PK: $Instructor$. $R_2(Course\_ID, Semester, Instructor, Room)$ with PK: $(Course\_ID, Semester)$ and FK: $Instructor$. 4. Verification: Lossless Join: $R_1 \cap R_2 = \{Instructor\}$, which is the primary key of $R_1$. Hence, the join is strictly lossless. Dependency Preserving: $Course\_ID, Semester \rightarrow Instructor, Room$ is preserved in $R_2$, and $Instructor \rightarrow Instructor\_Dept$ is preserved in $R_1$. All dependencies are preserved.

title: The table Faculty_Skill(Faculty, Skill, Teaching_Medium) stores all combinations of skills and teaching mediums (spoken languages) of each faculty member: F1 | Java | English; F1 | Java | Hindi; F1 | SQL | English; F1 | SQL | Hindi; F2 | Python | English. Identify the multivalued dependencies, explain why the table is not in 4NF, and decompose it into 4NF. Show that the natural join of the decomposed tables gives back the original table.
chunks: 1. Multivalued Dependencies (MVDs): For each faculty member, their programming skills and spoken languages (teaching mediums) are completely independent facts. Therefore, the MVDs are: $Faculty \twoheadrightarrow Skill$ and $Faculty \twoheadrightarrow Teaching\_Medium$ . 2. Why the Table Violates 4NF: The candidate key of the table is all three attributes combined: $(Faculty, Skill, Teaching\_Medium)$. In the non-trivial MVD $Faculty \twoheadrightarrow Skill$, the determinant $Faculty$ is NOT a super key . Hence, it violates 4NF, causing Cartesian product redundancy. 3. Decomposition into 4NF: Decompose into two independent relations: $R_1(Faculty, Skill)$: {(F1, Java), (F1, SQL), (F2, Python)} $R_2(Faculty, Teaching\_Medium)$: {(F1, English), (F1, Hindi), (F2, English)} 4. Verification of Lossless Natural Join ($R_1 \bowtie R_2$): For faculty F1 : Joining {(F1, Java), (F1, SQL)} with {(F1, English), (F1, Hindi)} yields: (F1, Java, English) , (F1, Java, Hindi) , (F1, SQL, English) , (F1, SQL, Hindi) . For faculty F2 : Joining {(F2, Python)} with {(F2, English)} yields (F2, Python, English) . The natural join reproduces the exact original table without loss or spurious tuples.

title: Design an E-R diagram for a Railway Reservation System that stores information about Passengers, Trains, Stations, Tickets and the schedule of trains at stations. Show all attributes, keys, relationships and mapping cardinalities.
chunks: Comprehensive E-R Model for a Railway Reservation System : Entity Sets & Attributes: Passenger : PNR_No (PK), Name, Age, Gender, Contact_No. Train : Train_No (PK), Train_Name, Train_Type (Express/Superfast). Station : Station_Code (PK), Station_Name, City, State. Ticket : Ticket_No (PK), Seat_No, Coach, Class (1AC/2AC/Sleeper), Fare, Travel_Date. Train_Schedule (Weak entity / Relationship table): Train_No (FK), Station_Code (FK), Arrival_Time, Departure_Time, Stop_Sequence. Relationships & Cardinalities: Books (Passenger - Ticket): 1:N (A passenger books 1 or more tickets; a ticket is issued to one passenger). Valid_For (Ticket - Train): N:1 (Multiple tickets are issued for a train journey). Stops_At (Train - Station): M:N through Train_Schedule (A train stops at multiple stations; a station serves multiple trains). Relational Mapping: Passenger(PNR_No [PK], Name, Age, Gender, Phone) Train(Train_No [PK], Train_Name, Train_Type) Station(Station_Code [PK], Station_Name, City) Train_Schedule(Train_No [PK, FK], Station_Code [PK, FK], Arr_Time, Dep_Time, Seq_No) Ticket(Ticket_No [PK], PNR_No [FK], Train_No [FK], Coach, Seat, Fare, Travel_Date)

title: For the relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with the functional dependency set F = {A -> B, BC -> D, D -> E, E -> C}, find all candidate keys, list the prime and non-prime attributes, and state, with justification, the highest normal form satisfied by R.
chunks: Given: $R(A, B, C, D, E)$ and $F = \{A \rightarrow B,\, BC \rightarrow D,\, D \rightarrow E,\, E \rightarrow C\}$. 1. Candidate Keys Determination: $A$ never appears on the RHS of any FD, so $A$ must be in every candidate key. Test combinations with $A$: $(AC)^+$: $AC \rightarrow B$ (via $A \rightarrow B$) $\rightarrow D$ (via $BC \rightarrow D$) $\rightarrow E$ (via $D \rightarrow E$). So $(AC)^+ = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$. $\implies \mathbf{AC}$ is a candidate key. Since $E \rightarrow C$, replace $C$ with $E$: $(AE)^+ = \{A, E, C, B, D\} = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$. $\implies \mathbf{AE}$ is a candidate key. Since $D \rightarrow E$, replace $E$ with $D$: $(AD)^+ = \{A, D, E, C, B\} = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$. $\implies \mathbf{AD}$ is a candidate key. Candidate Keys: AC , AD , and AE . 2. Prime and Non-Prime Attributes: Prime Attributes: $\{A, C, D, E\}$ (Members of at least one candidate key). Non-Prime Attributes: $\{B\}$ (Does not belong to any candidate key). 3. Highest Normal Form Satisfied: 1NF: Satisfied. 2NF Check: A partial dependency occurs if a non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. Here, the non-prime attribute is $B$. In $A \rightarrow B$, $A$ is a proper subset of candidate keys $AC, AD, AE$. Thus, $A \rightarrow B$ is a partial dependency! Therefore, $R$ violates 2NF. The highest normal form satisfied by R is 1NF.

title: Map the following E-R design into relational tables: an entity Student(Roll_No, Name, {Phone}, DOB, Age), where Phone is multivalued and Age is derived from DOB; an entity Course(Course_ID, Title); a many-to-many relationship Enrolls between Student and Course with the attribute Grade; and a weak entity Dependent(Dep_Name, Relation) that depends on Student. Show the resulting tables with their primary and foreign keys and explain how the multivalued, derived and weak-entity features were handled.
chunks: Relational Table Mapping: -- 1. Regular Entity Student (Derived attribute Age omitted, Phone separated) CREATE TABLE Student ( Roll_No INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(100), DOB DATE ); -- 2. Multivalued Attribute Phone (Forms separate table with owner PK) CREATE TABLE Student_Phone ( Roll_No INT, Phone VARCHAR(15), PRIMARY KEY (Roll_No, Phone), FOREIGN KEY (Roll_No) REFERENCES Student(Roll_No) ON DELETE CASCADE ); -- 3. Regular Entity Course CREATE TABLE Course ( Course_ID VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(100) ); -- 4. Many-to-Many Relationship Enrolls CREATE TABLE Enrolls ( Roll_No INT, Course_ID VARCHAR(10), Grade CHAR(2), PRIMARY KEY (Roll_No, Course_ID), FOREIGN KEY (Roll_No) REFERENCES Student(Roll_No), FOREIGN KEY (Course_ID) REFERENCES Course(Course_ID) ); -- 5. Weak Entity Dependent (Owner PK + Partial Key) CREATE TABLE Dependent ( Roll_No INT, Dep_Name VARCHAR(50), Relation VARCHAR(50), PRIMARY KEY (Roll_No, Dep_Name), FOREIGN KEY (Roll_No) REFERENCES Student(Roll_No) ON DELETE CASCADE ); Handling of Special Features: Multivalued Attribute ( Phone ): Mapped to a distinct table Student_Phone(Roll_No, Phone) with a composite primary key. Derived Attribute ( Age ): Excluded from storage to avoid redundancy; dynamically computed on-the-fly using DATEDIFF(CURRENT_DATE, DOB) . Weak Entity ( Dependent ): Includes the primary key of its identifying owner entity ( Student.Roll_No ) combined with its discriminator ( Dep_Name ) to form the primary key.

title: The relation Employee_Project(EmpID, ProjID, EmpName, ProjName, Role, DeptID, DeptName) has the functional dependencies {EmpID -> EmpName, EmpID -> DeptID, DeptID -> DeptName, ProjID -> ProjName, (EmpID, ProjID) -> Role}. Find the candidate key, analyse the insertion, update and deletion anomalies present in the relation with one example each, and normalize the relation step by step up to 3NF.
chunks: 1. Candidate Key: (EmpID, ProjID)+ = {EmpID, ProjID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName, ProjName, Role} . Unique Candidate Key is (EmpID, ProjID) . 2. Modification Anomalies in the Unnormalized Table: Insertion Anomaly: Cannot insert a new employee who has not yet been assigned to a project, because ProjID is part of the primary key and cannot be NULL. Update Anomaly: If department name for DeptID = D1 changes, every row where an employee belongs to D1 must be updated; missing any row causes data inconsistency. Deletion Anomaly: If the sole employee working on project P9 is deleted, all project details for P9 are permanently lost. 3. Step-by-Step Normalization: Step A: 2NF Decomposition (Eliminate Partial Dependencies): $R_{Emp}(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName)$ (Eliminates $EmpID \rightarrow EmpName, DeptID$) $R_{Proj}(ProjID, ProjName)$ (Eliminates $ProjID \rightarrow ProjName$) $R_{Assign}(EmpID, ProjID, Role)$ (Full key dependency) Step B: 3NF Decomposition (Eliminate Transitive Dependency in $R_{Emp}$): In $R_{Emp}$, $EmpID \rightarrow DeptID \rightarrow DeptName$ is transitive. Decompose $R_{Emp}$ into: Department(DeptID, DeptName) - PK: DeptID Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID) - PK: EmpID , FK: DeptID Final 3NF Schema: Department , Employee , Project , and Assignment .

title: The relation SPJ(Supplier, Part, Project) satisfies the join dependency that it is the join of its projections (Supplier, Part), (Part, Project) and (Project, Supplier). Explain the concept of join dependency and fifth normal form (5NF), analyse why SPJ is not in 5NF, and decompose it. Show how the decomposition removes redundancy and why the join of the three projections must be lossless.
chunks: 1. Join Dependency (JD) & Fifth Normal Form (5NF): A relation $R$ satisfies the Join Dependency $\bowtie(R_1, R_2, \dots, R_n)$ if and only if $R$ is equal to the natural join of its projections $R_1, R_2, \dots, R_n$. Fifth Normal Form (5NF / Project-Join Normal Form): A relation is in 5NF if and only if it is in 4NF and every non-trivial join dependency $\bowtie(R_1, R_2, \dots, R_n)$ in $R$ is implied by the candidate keys of $R$ (i.e., every $R_i$ contains a candidate key of $R$). 2. Why SPJ is not in 5NF: In SPJ(Supplier, Part, Project) , the only candidate key is the composite key (Supplier, Part, Project) . The business rule states that whenever Supplier $S$ supplies Part $P$, Part $P$ is used in Project $J$, and Supplier $S$ supplies Project $J$, then $S$ MUST supply $P$ to $J$. This cyclic constraint is a non-trivial Join Dependency: $\bowtie((Supplier, Part), (Part, Project), (Project, Supplier))$. Since none of the projections $(Supplier, Part)$, $(Part, Project)$, or $(Project, Supplier)$ is a super key of SPJ , SPJ violates 5NF . 3. Decomposition into 5NF: Decompose into three binary projection relations: SP(Supplier, Part) PJ(Part, Project) JS(Project, Supplier) 4. Lossless Reconstruction & Redundancy Removal: Storing binary projections eliminates cyclic redundant combinations and avoids spurious tuples during three-way join. The natural join $SP \bowtie PJ \bowtie JS$ exactly reconstructs the original valid ternary tuples without information loss.

title: Distinguish between DDL and DML statements, giving one example command for each.
chunks: Comparison between DDL and DML statements in SQL: Feature Data Definition Language (DDL) Data Manipulation Language (DML) Purpose Used to define, alter, and manage database structural objects (tables, schemas, indexes). Used to retrieve, insert, modify, and delete the actual data records stored within tables. Commit Behavior Auto-committed permanently; cannot be rolled back in most RDBMS. Not auto-committed by default; can be committed or rolled back using TCL. Example Command CREATE TABLE Student (RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50)); INSERT INTO Student VALUES (101, 'Rahul'); or SELECT * FROM Student;

title: Briefly explain generalization and specialization in an extended E-R model.
chunks: Concepts in the Extended E-R (EER) model: Generalization (Bottom-Up): An abstraction process where multiple lower-level entity sets sharing common attributes and relationships are synthesized into a generalized higher-level entity set. Example: Synthesizing Car and Truck into the generalized entity Vehicle . Specialization (Top-Down): The inverse process where sub-groupings within a higher-level entity set that possess distinct, specialized attributes or relationships are separated into lower-level entity sets. Example: Sub-classing Employee into specialized entities Hourly_Employee and Salaried_Employee .

title: List any four SQL aggregate functions and state what each computes.
chunks: Four common SQL aggregate functions and their computations: COUNT(column) : Computes the total number of non-NULL values in a column (or COUNT(*) for total rows including NULLs). SUM(column) : Computes the mathematical sum of all numeric values in a column, ignoring NULLs. AVG(column) : Computes the arithmetic mean of all numeric values in a column, ignoring NULLs. MAX(column) / MIN(column) : Computes the maximum (or minimum) value in a numeric, string, or date column.

title: Distinguish between a DBMS and an RDBMS.
chunks: Comparison between DBMS and RDBMS: Feature DBMS Relational DBMS (RDBMS) Data Storage Structure Stores data in hierarchical trees, graphs, or flat files. Stores data in tabular 2D relations (tables with rows and columns). Relationships & Integrity Relationships between data entities are maintained manually or programmatically; lacks foreign key constraints. Formal foreign key constraints enforce referential integrity across related tables. Normalization & Rules Does not follow Codd's 12 rules; prone to redundancy. Strictly adheres to Codd's relational rules and normal forms (1NF-BCNF). Software Examples XML databases, FileMaker, dBase. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server.

title: List any four fundamental operators of relational algebra and state the purpose of each.
chunks: Four fundamental operators of Relational Algebra: Select ($\sigma$): A unary operator that filters tuples (rows) from a relation that satisfy a specified predicate/condition (e.g., $\sigma_{salary > 50000}(Employee)$). Project ($\pi$): A unary operator that extracts specified columns (attributes) from a relation, automatically discarding duplicate tuples (e.g., $\pi_{ename, salary}(Employee)$). Cartesian Product ($\times$): A binary operator that pairs every tuple of relation $R$ with every tuple of relation $S$ (yields $|R| \times |S|$ tuples). Union ($\cup$): A binary operator that combines tuples from two union-compatible relations, eliminating duplicates (e.g., $R \cup S$).

title: Differentiate between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause in SQL with an example.
chunks: Comparison between WHERE and HAVING clauses: Feature WHERE Clause HAVING Clause Application Filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation takes place. Filters groups of rows after the GROUP BY aggregation is calculated. Aggregate Functions Cannot contain aggregate functions directly (e.g., WHERE AVG(sal) > 5000 is illegal). Designed specifically to evaluate conditions with aggregate functions (e.g., HAVING AVG(sal) > 5000 ). Usage with GROUP BY Can be used with or without GROUP BY . Almost always used alongside GROUP BY . Example: SELECT Dept, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Status = 'Active' -- WHERE filters rows before aggregation GROUP BY Dept HAVING AVG(Salary) > 60000; -- HAVING filters summarized group averages

title: Define entity, entity set and relationship set with one example each.
chunks: Fundamental concepts in ER Modeling: Entity: A distinct real-world object, person, place, or concept that is distinguishable from other objects (e.g., an individual student named 'Asha' with RollNo 101). Entity Set: A collection or set of all similar entities sharing the same properties or attributes (e.g., the set of all students in a university, represented as Student ). Relationship Set: A mathematical set of relationships of the same type connecting entities from two or more entity sets (e.g., the relationship set Enrolls connecting entities from Student and Course ).

title: Given the table Employee(eid, ename, dept, salary), write SQL queries to (i) show departments with average salary > 50000, (ii) find the second highest salary without using LIMIT, and (iii) list employees whose name starts with 'A' and ends with 'n'.
chunks: SQL solutions for the table Employee(eid, ename, dept, salary) : (i) Departments with average salary > 50,000: SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM Employee GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000; (ii) Second highest salary without LIMIT: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest_salary FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee); (iii) Employees whose name starts with 'A' and ends with 'n': SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE ename LIKE 'A%n';

title: Using the relations Student(sid, sname, age, city), Course(cid, cname, credits) and Enrollment(sid, cid, grade), write relational algebra expressions to (i) find names of students from 'Delhi' with age > 20, (ii) find names of students enrolled in 'DBMS', and (iii) find courses with credits > 3 that no student has enrolled in.
chunks: Relational algebra expressions: (i) Names of students from 'Delhi' with age > 20: $$\pi_{sname}(\sigma_{city = \text{'Delhi'} \,\land\, age > 20}(Student))$$ (ii) Names of students enrolled in 'DBMS': $$\pi_{sname}(Student \bowtie Enrollment \bowtie \sigma_{cname = \text{'DBMS'}}(Course))$$ (iii) Courses with credits > 3 that no student has enrolled in: $$\pi_{cid, cname}(\sigma_{credits > 3}(Course)) - \pi_{cid, cname}(\sigma_{credits > 3}(Course) \bowtie Enrollment)$$

title: Explain INNER JOIN, LEFT OUTER JOIN and RIGHT OUTER JOIN with an example for each.
chunks: Comparison of SQL Join types using sample tables A(id, val) = {(1, X), (2, Y)} and B(id, desc) = {(1, M), (3, N)} : INNER JOIN: Returns only matching rows that satisfy the join condition in both tables. Unmatched rows are eliminated. Result: (1, X, M) LEFT OUTER JOIN: Returns all rows from the left table, along with matching rows from the right table. For unmatched left rows, right columns are populated with NULL . Result: (1, X, M) , (2, Y, NULL) RIGHT OUTER JOIN: Returns all rows from the right table, along with matching rows from the left table. For unmatched right rows, left columns are populated with NULL . Result: (1, X, M) , (3, NULL, N) -- Syntax Example SELECT A.id, A.val, B.desc FROM A LEFT OUTER JOIN B ON A.id = B.id;

title: Define a view. Give two benefits of using views and illustrate, with an example, when a view cannot be updated directly.
chunks: A View in SQL is a virtual table whose contents are defined dynamically by a stored SELECT query. It does not store physical data records of its own (except materialized views); rather, it computes results on-the-fly from underlying base tables. Two Key Benefits: Data Security: Hides sensitive columns (e.g., salaries, passwords) by exposing only permitted columns to specific user roles. Query Simplification: Encapsulates complex joins, subqueries, and calculations into a simple virtual table name. When a View Cannot Be Updated Directly: A view cannot be updated directly if its definition involves aggregate functions, GROUP BY , DISTINCT , or UNION , because the database cannot map changes in an aggregated value back to a unique row in the base table: CREATE VIEW Dept_Salaries AS SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM Employee GROUP BY dept; -- ILLEGAL: Cannot update an aggregated group average UPDATE Dept_Salaries SET avg_sal = 75000 WHERE dept = 'IT';

title: For the table PRODUCT_MAST(Product_ID, Product_Name, Price), write SQL queries to (i) find products priced above the overall average price, (ii) display product names in uppercase with price rounded to nearest integer, and (iii) count distinct price points.
chunks: SQL queries for PRODUCT_MAST(Product_ID, Product_Name, Price) : (i) Products priced above the overall average price: SELECT Product_ID, Product_Name, Price FROM PRODUCT_MAST WHERE Price > (SELECT AVG(Price) FROM PRODUCT_MAST); (ii) Product names in uppercase with price rounded to the nearest integer: SELECT UPPER(Product_Name) AS Prod_Upper, ROUND(Price) AS Rounded_Price FROM PRODUCT_MAST; (iii) Count distinct price points: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT Price) AS Unique_Price_Count FROM PRODUCT_MAST;

title: Create a view over the tables Student, Course and Enrollment (Student(sid, sname, age, city), Course(cid, cname, credits), Enrollment(sid, cid, grade)) that displays sid, sname, cname and grade for all passing grades (grade != 'F'). Then show how a user can query this view to find all passing courses for student sid = 101.
chunks: 1. View Creation: CREATE VIEW Passing_Students_View AS SELECT s.sid, s.sname, c.cname, e.grade FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE e.grade != 'F'; 2. Querying the View for sid = 101 : SELECT cname, grade FROM Passing_Students_View WHERE sid = 101; This query simplifies access by avoiding repeating multi-table joins while automatically filtering out failing grades.

title: For the table Book(Book_ID, Title, Price, Stock), write SQL commands to (i) insert a new book record, (ii) increase price by 10% for books with stock < 5, and (iii) delete books that have zero stock and price > 1000.
chunks: SQL commands for Book(Book_ID, Title, Price, Stock) : (i) Insert a new book record: INSERT INTO Book (Book_ID, Title, Price, Stock) VALUES (101, 'Database System Concepts', 650.00, 25); (ii) Increase price by 10% for books with stock < 5: UPDATE Book SET Price = Price * 1.10 WHERE Stock < 5; (iii) Delete books with zero stock and price > 1000: DELETE FROM Book WHERE Stock = 0 AND Price > 1000;

title: Using Student(sid, sname, age, city), Course(cid, cname, credits) and Enrollment(sid, cid, grade), write SQL queries to (i) find the name of students who have enrolled in both 'DBMS' and 'OS', and (ii) find students who have enrolled in all courses.
chunks: SQL solutions: (i) Students enrolled in BOTH 'DBMS' and 'OS' (Intersection): SELECT s.sname FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS' INTERSECT SELECT s.sname FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE c.cname = 'OS'; (Alternative using subquery): SELECT sname FROM Student WHERE sid IN ( SELECT sid FROM Enrollment JOIN Course USING(cid) WHERE cname = 'DBMS' ) AND sid IN ( SELECT sid FROM Enrollment JOIN Course USING(cid) WHERE cname = 'OS' ); (ii) Students enrolled in ALL courses (Relational Division): SELECT s.sname FROM Student s WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT c.cid FROM Course c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT e.cid FROM Enrollment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid AND e.cid = c.cid ) );

title: Explain the DCL commands GRANT and REVOKE with examples, including the use of WITH GRANT OPTION.
chunks: Data Control Language (DCL) manages security permissions on database objects: GRANT : Allocates privileges (such as SELECT , INSERT , UPDATE ) on tables/views to specific users or roles. GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON Employee TO user_ravi; WITH GRANT OPTION : Enables the grantee to grant those same privileges to other users. GRANT SELECT ON Employee TO user_ravi WITH GRANT OPTION; -- user_ravi can now grant SELECT on Employee to user_priya REVOKE : Withdraws previously allocated privileges from a user or role. REVOKE INSERT ON Employee FROM user_ravi; Cascading Revoke: If WITH GRANT OPTION privileges are revoked with CASCADE , privileges granted down the chain to other users are revoked automatically.

title: Consider the table Employee(eid, ename, dept, salary). Write SQL queries to (i) find the maximum salary in each department, (ii) display departments having more than 5 employees, and (iii) show all employees whose salary is above the average salary of their respective department.
chunks: SQL solutions for Employee(eid, ename, dept, salary) : (i) Maximum salary in each department: SELECT dept, MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM Employee GROUP BY dept; (ii) Departments having more than 5 employees: SELECT dept, COUNT(eid) AS emp_count FROM Employee GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(eid) > 5; (iii) Employees whose salary is above their department's average (Correlated Subquery): SELECT e.eid, e.ename, e.dept, e.salary FROM Employee e WHERE e.salary > ( SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM Employee e2 WHERE e2.dept = e.dept );

title: Differentiate between tuple relational calculus and domain relational calculus. Give the formal expression in each for finding the names of employees earning > 40000 from Employee(eid, ename, salary).
chunks: Comparison between Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) and Domain Relational Calculus (DRC): Feature Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) Domain Relational Calculus (DRC) Variable Representation Variables range over tuples (rows) of a relation. Variables range over domains (individual attribute columns) . Notation $\{t \mid P(t)\}$ where $t$ is a tuple variable. $\{\langle x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n \rangle \mid P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)\}$. Query Nature Non-procedural / Declarative. Non-procedural / Declarative. Formal Expressions for employees with salary > 40,000: In TRC: $$\{t.ename \mid t \in Employee \land t.salary > 40000\}$$ In DRC: $$\{\langle n \rangle \mid \exists i, s \, (\langle i, n, s \rangle \in Employee \land s > 40000)\}$$

title: Consider the table Employee(EID, EName, ManagerID), where ManagerID refers to the EID of the manager. Write a SQL query using SELF JOIN to display each employee's name along with their manager's name, and explain how an employee without a manager (e.g. CEO) can be included.
chunks: 1. Self Join Query (Inner Join): SELECT e.EName AS Employee_Name, m.EName AS Manager_Name FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.ManagerID = m.EID; Here, the table Employee is joined with itself using aliases e (subordinate) and m (manager). 2. Including Employees Without a Manager (CEO): An inner join drops any employee whose ManagerID is NULL (such as the CEO). To include them, a LEFT OUTER JOIN must be used: SELECT e.EName AS Employee_Name, COALESCE(m.EName, 'Top Executive / CEO') AS Manager_Name FROM Employee e LEFT OUTER JOIN Employee m ON e.ManagerID = m.EID; This guarantees that every employee is displayed, displaying 'Top Executive / CEO' where ManagerID is NULL.

title: Using Student(sid, sname, age, city), Course(cid, cname, credits) and Enrollment(sid, cid, grade), write SQL queries to (i) find students enrolled in the maximum number of courses, (ii) find courses that have no 'F' grades recorded, (iii) compute average credits taken per student, and (iv) list courses with total enrollment higher than the average enrollment across all courses.
chunks: Comprehensive SQL solutions: (i) Students enrolled in the maximum number of courses: SELECT s.sid, s.sname, COUNT(e.cid) AS total_courses FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid GROUP BY s.sid, s.sname HAVING COUNT(e.cid) = ( SELECT MAX(cnt) FROM ( SELECT COUNT(cid) AS cnt FROM Enrollment GROUP BY sid ) AS t ); (ii) Courses with NO 'F' grades recorded: SELECT cid, cname FROM Course WHERE cid NOT IN ( SELECT cid FROM Enrollment WHERE grade = 'F' ); (iii) Compute average credits taken per student: SELECT AVG(total_cred) AS avg_credits_per_student FROM ( SELECT e.sid, SUM(c.credits) AS total_cred FROM Enrollment e JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid GROUP BY e.sid ) AS student_credits; (iv) Courses with enrollment higher than average course enrollment: SELECT c.cid, c.cname, COUNT(e.sid) AS enroll_count FROM Course c JOIN Enrollment e ON c.cid = e.cid GROUP BY c.cid, c.cname HAVING COUNT(e.sid) > ( SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM ( SELECT COUNT(sid) AS cnt FROM Enrollment GROUP BY cid ) AS avg_tbl );

title: Consider the relations Student(sid, sname, age, city), Course(cid, cname, credits) and Enrollment(sid, cid, grade). Write (i) a relational algebra expression to find the names of students enrolled in all courses with credits = 4, and (ii) a tuple relational calculus expression for the same.
chunks:
Given: Student(sid, sname, age, city) , Course(cid, cname, credits) , Enrollment(sid, cid, grade) . 1. Relational Algebra Expression (Relational Division $\div$): Let $C_4 = \pi_{cid}(\sigma_{credits = 4}(Course))$ be the set of all 4-credit courses. Let $SE = \pi_{sid, cid}(Enrollment)$ be student-course enrollment pairs. The set of student IDs enrolled in all 4-credit courses is obtained via division:$$S_{all} = SE \div C_4$$ Project student names by joining with Student :$$\mathbf{\pi_{sname}(Student  owtie (\pi_{sid, cid}(Enrollment) \div \pi_{cid}(\sigma_{credits = 4}(Course))))}$$ 2. Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) Expression: Using universal quantification ($ orall$): Find students $s$ such that for every course $c$ with credits $= 4$, there exists an enrollment $e$ for student $s$ in course $c$: $$\{s.sname \mid s \in Student \land  orall c \in Course \,(c.credits = 4 \implies \exists e \in Enrollment \,(e.sid = s.sid \land e.cid = c.cid))\}$$ Equivalent form using negation ($
eg \exists$): $$\{s.sname \mid s \in Student \land 
eg \exists c \in Course \,(c.credits = 4 \land 
eg \exists e \in Enrollment \,(e.sid = s.sid \land e.cid = c.cid))\}$$

title: Consider the tables Employee(EID, EName, DID) = {(1, Asha, 10), (2, Ravi, 20), (3, Meera, NULL)} and Department(DID, DName) = {(10, IT), (20, HR), (30, Finance)}. Show the exact output relation (with all rows and columns) for (i) Natural Join, (ii) Left Outer Join, (iii) Right Outer Join, (iv) Full Outer Join, and (v) Cartesian Product.

title: In a company, Employees work on Projects and every (Employee, Project) assignment has hours worked. (i) Write SQL to create tables Employee, Project and Works_On with suitable constraints, (ii) write SQL to find projects with total hours > 500, and (iii) write a query to find employees who work on all projects located in 'Mumbai'.
chunks: (i) Table Creation with Integrity Constraints: CREATE TABLE Employee ( EID INT PRIMARY KEY, EName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Salary DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (Salary > 0) ); CREATE TABLE Project ( PID INT PRIMARY KEY, PName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Location VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Works_On ( EID INT, PID INT, Hours DECIMAL(5,2) CHECK (Hours >= 0), PRIMARY KEY (EID, PID), FOREIGN KEY (EID) REFERENCES Employee(EID) ON DELETE CASCADE, FOREIGN KEY (PID) REFERENCES Project(PID) ON DELETE CASCADE ); (ii) Projects with total hours > 500: SELECT p.PID, p.PName, SUM(w.Hours) AS Total_Hours FROM Project p JOIN Works_On w ON p.PID = w.PID GROUP BY p.PID, p.PName HAVING SUM(w.Hours) > 500; (iii) Employees who work on ALL projects located in 'Mumbai': SELECT e.EID, e.EName FROM Employee e WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT p.PID FROM Project p WHERE p.Location = 'Mumbai' AND NOT EXISTS ( SELECT w.PID FROM Works_On w WHERE w.EID = e.EID AND w.PID = p.PID ) );

title: Given Employee(emp_id, emp_name, salary, dept_id) and Department(dept_id, dept_name, location), write SQL queries to (i) find the highest paid employee in each department, (ii) display departments where no employee is currently assigned, (iii) increase salary by 5% for all employees in the 'Sales' department, and (iv) find employees who earn more than their manager.
chunks: SQL solutions: (i) Highest paid employee in each department (Correlated Subquery): SELECT e.emp_id, e.emp_name, e.dept_id, e.salary FROM Employee e WHERE e.salary = ( SELECT MAX(e2.salary) FROM Employee e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id ); (ii) Departments where no employee is currently assigned: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name FROM Department d LEFT JOIN Employee e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id WHERE e.emp_id IS NULL; (iii) Increase salary by 5% for employees in 'Sales' department: UPDATE Employee SET salary = salary * 1.05 WHERE dept_id = ( SELECT dept_id FROM Department WHERE dept_name = 'Sales' ); (iv) Employees who earn more than their manager (Self Join): SELECT e.emp_name AS Employee, e.salary AS Emp_Salary, m.emp_name AS Manager, m.salary AS Mgr_Salary FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

title: Given the relations R(A, B) = {(1, a), (2, b), (3, c)} and S(A, B) = {(2, b), (3, d), (4, e)}, compute the result of (i) R UNION S, (ii) R INTERSECT S, and (iii) R - S.
chunks: Computations for $R(A, B)$ and $S(A, B)$: (i) $R \cup S$ (Union): Combines all distinct tuples, removing duplicates:$$\mathbf{R \cup S = \{(1, a),\, (2, b),\, (3, c),\, (3, d),\, (4, e)\}}$$ (ii) $R \cap S$ (Intersection): Returns tuples that appear in both relations:$$\mathbf{R \cap S = \{(2, b)\}}$$ (iii) $R - S$ (Set Difference): Returns tuples present in $R$ but absent in $S$:$$\mathbf{R - S = \{(1, a),\, (3, c)\}}$$

title: Consider the following queries on Student(sid, sname, age, city) and Enrollment(sid, cid, grade): (i) write a query using EXISTS to find students enrolled in cid = 'C101', (ii) rewrite it using IN, (iii) write a query using NOT EXISTS to find students not enrolled in any course, and (iv) compare the query execution performance between EXISTS and IN with NULL values.
chunks: (i) Query using EXISTS : SELECT s.sid, s.sname FROM Student s WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Enrollment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid AND e.cid = 'C101' ); (ii) Equivalent Query using IN : SELECT sid, sname FROM Student WHERE sid IN ( SELECT sid FROM Enrollment WHERE cid = 'C101' ); (iii) Query using NOT EXISTS for unenrolled students: SELECT s.sid, s.sname FROM Student s WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Enrollment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid ); (iv) Performance Comparison & NULL Value Pitfall: Short-Circuit Evaluation: EXISTS terminates immediately upon finding the first matching row (returns boolean TRUE), making it faster on large subqueries with indexes. The NULL Hazard in NOT IN : If the subquery in NOT IN returns even a single NULL value, the entire NOT IN condition evaluates to UNKNOWN , returning zero rows . In contrast, NOT EXISTS safely checks for presence/absence of rows and is completely immune to NULL subquery values.

title: Consider Student(SID, SName, Dept_ID) and Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), where Dept_ID in Student is a foreign key. (i) Explain referential integrity, (ii) describe what happens when a department row is deleted under RESTRICT, CASCADE, and SET NULL, and (iii) show the SQL DDL syntax for ON DELETE CASCADE and ON UPDATE SET NULL.
chunks: (i) Referential Integrity: Referential Integrity is a relational database constraint requiring that any foreign key value in a referencing table (e.g., Student.Dept_ID ) must either match a valid primary key value in the referenced table ( Department.Dept_ID ) or be NULL . It prevents dangling pointers and orphaned records. (ii) Actions on Deleting a Department Row: ON DELETE RESTRICT (or NO ACTION ): The database rejects and aborts the deletion if any student rows currently reference that department. ON DELETE CASCADE : Automatically deletes all student rows associated with the deleted department. ON DELETE SET NULL : Automatically sets the Dept_ID column to NULL for all student rows that referenced the deleted department (requires column to be nullable). (iii) SQL DDL Syntax: CREATE TABLE Student ( SID INT PRIMARY KEY, SName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Dept_ID INT, CONSTRAINT fk_student_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE SET NULL );

title: Consider the tables Patient(pid, pname, age, city), Doctor(did, dname, speciality) and Consults(pid, did, consult_date, fee). Write SQL queries to (i) find doctors who have consulted more than 10 distinct patients, (ii) compute the total consultation fees earned by each doctor, (iii) find patients who have consulted doctors in both 'Cardiology' and 'Neurology', and (iv) list patients who have never consulted any doctor.
chunks: SQL queries for the Healthcare database: (i) Doctors who consulted more than 10 distinct patients: SELECT d.did, d.dname, COUNT(DISTINCT c.pid) AS unique_patients FROM Doctor d JOIN Consults c ON d.did = c.did GROUP BY d.did, d.dname HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.pid) > 10; (ii) Total consultation fees earned by each doctor: SELECT d.did, d.dname, COALESCE(SUM(c.fee), 0) AS total_earnings FROM Doctor d LEFT JOIN Consults c ON d.did = c.did GROUP BY d.did, d.dname; (iii) Patients who consulted both Cardiology and Neurology: SELECT p.pid, p.pname FROM Patient p WHERE p.pid IN ( SELECT c.pid FROM Consults c JOIN Doctor d ON c.did = d.did WHERE d.speciality = 'Cardiology' ) AND p.pid IN ( SELECT c.pid FROM Consults c JOIN Doctor d ON c.did = d.did WHERE d.speciality = 'Neurology' ); (iv) Patients who have never consulted any doctor: SELECT p.pid, p.pname FROM Patient p LEFT JOIN Consults c ON p.pid = c.pid WHERE c.pid IS NULL;

title: A university database stores Person(pid, name, address). A person is a Student (with roll_no, cgpa), a Faculty (with emp_no, salary, rank) or an Alumnus (with grad_year, degree). (i) Draw an EER diagram illustrating specialization/generalization with disjoint and total participation constraints, and (ii) explain the three different mapping options for converting specialization hierarchies into relational tables.
chunks: (i) EER Diagram (Specialization Hierarchy): (ii) Three Relational Mapping Options: Option 1: Multiple Tables for Superclass and Subclasses: Create Person(pid, name, address) , Student(pid, roll_no, cgpa) , Faculty(pid, emp_no, salary, rank) , Alumnus(pid, grad_year, degree) where subclass tables have primary keys that are foreign keys to Person.pid . Ideal for disjoint/overlap with specific attributes. Fast queries with zero joins, but wastes storage with NULL values.

title: Consider the relation R(A, B, C) with the functional dependency set F = {A -> B}. Analyse whether the decomposition into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C) is (i) lossless join, and (ii) dependency preserving. Justify your answer using Heath's theorem and the definition of dependency preservation.
chunks: Given: $R(A, B, C)$, $F = \{A \rightarrow B\}$, decomposed into $R_1(A, B)$ and $R_2(B, C)$. 1. Lossless Join Analysis (Heath's Theorem): Heath's Theorem states that a binary decomposition of $R$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless if and only if the common attribute set ($R_1 \cap R_2$) functionally determines either $R_1$ or $R_2$, i.e.:$$(R_1 \cap R_2) \rightarrow R_1 \quad \text{OR} \quad (R_1 \cap R_2) \rightarrow R_2$$ Here, $R_1 \cap R_2 = \{B\}$. We compute the attribute closure of the common attribute $B$ with respect to $F$:$$B^+ = \{B\}$$ Since $B^+$ does not contain $A$ ($B \not\rightarrow A$) and does not contain $C$ ($B \not\rightarrow C$), $B$ is NOT a super key of either $R_1$ or $R_2$. Conclusion: The decomposition is LOSSY (Not Lossless)! Joining $R_1 \bowtie R_2$ will generate spurious tuples. 2. Dependency Preservation Analysis: $F_1 = \pi_{R_1}(F) = \{A \rightarrow B\}$ (since both $A, B \in R_1$). $F_2 = \pi_{R_2}(F) = \emptyset$. $(F_1 \cup F_2)^+ = \{A \rightarrow B\}^+ = F^+$. Conclusion: The decomposition IS DEPENDENCY PRESERVING.

title: List any four constraints that can be applied on a table in SQL.
chunks: Four essential integrity constraints in SQL are: PRIMARY KEY : Uniquely identifies each record in a table; automatically enforces uniqueness and forbids NULL values. FOREIGN KEY : Enforces referential integrity by ensuring that values in the referencing column match a primary key in the referenced parent table or are NULL . UNIQUE : Ensures that all values in a column or set of columns are distinct; permits multiple NULL values in standard SQL. CHECK : Ensures that all values stored in a column satisfy a specific logical condition (e.g., CHECK (Salary > 0) ).

title: Differentiate between UNION and UNION ALL in SQL.
chunks: Comparison between UNION and UNION ALL: Feature UNION UNION ALL Duplicate Handling Combines results from multiple SELECT queries and eliminates duplicate rows . Combines results from multiple SELECT queries and retains all duplicate rows . Sorting & Overhead Performs an internal sort / hash operation to identify and remove duplicates, resulting in higher execution overhead. Appends rows directly without sorting or hashing, executing significantly faster. Usage Recommendation Used when unique mathematical set union is required. Used when duplicates are permissible or when datasets are known to be mutually disjoint.

title: Define a trigger. Distinguish between a BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger.
chunks: A Trigger in SQL is a specialized stored procedure that executes (fires) automatically in response to a specified database event (such as INSERT , UPDATE , or DELETE ) on a particular table. BEFORE vs. AFTER Triggers: BEFORE Trigger: Fires prior to the execution of the triggering DML statement. Typically used for input validation, data sanitization, or modifying column values (via NEW.column ) before committing them to storage. AFTER Trigger: Fires subsequent to the completion of the triggering DML statement. Used for maintaining audit trails, propagating cascade updates to other tables, or logging historical changes.

title: What is a sequence (or AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL)? Mention one situation where it is used.
chunks: A Sequence (or AUTO_INCREMENT attribute in MySQL) is a database object that automatically generates a unique sequential integer sequence according to specified step increments (typically incrementing by 1 for each new row inserted). Primary Situation of Use: Generating Surrogate Primary Keys (synthetic identifiers) for tables that lack a natural, immutable candidate key, such as Order_ID in an orders table or User_ID in a customer registration portal, ensuring uniqueness without requiring manual ID entry.

title: List any four string functions in SQL and state the purpose of each.
chunks: Four essential SQL string functions and their operations: UPPER(str) / LOWER(str) : Converts all characters in a string to uppercase (or lowercase) for standardized formatting. LENGTH(str) (or LEN(str) ): Returns the total number of characters in the string. SUBSTRING(str, pos, len) (or SUBSTR ): Extracts and returns a substring starting at character position pos for a length of len characters. CONCAT(str1, str2, ...) : Concatenates two or more strings together into a single combined string output.

title: Differentiate between the DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP commands.
chunks: Comparison between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP: Feature DELETE TRUNCATE DROP Command Type DML (Data Manipulation) DDL (Data Definition) DDL (Data Definition) Scope Removes specific rows (filtered via WHERE ) or all rows. Removes all rows from the table in one operation. Table Structure Preserved intact. Preserved intact; resets auto-increment counters. Completely deleted from the database catalog. Performance Slower (deletes and logs row-by-row). Very fast (deallocates entire data pages). Fastest (drops structural schema). Rollback Can be rolled back in transactions. Cannot be rolled back in most RDBMS (auto-committed). Cannot be rolled back.

title: Differentiate between the UNIQUE constraint and the PRIMARY KEY constraint.
chunks: Comparison between UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints: Feature PRIMARY KEY Constraint UNIQUE Constraint NULL Values Strictly forbids NULL values (every tuple must have a known non-null key value). Allows NULL values (in standard SQL, multiple rows may contain NULL ). Table Limit A table can have at most one Primary Key. A table can have multiple Unique constraints defined across different columns. Default Index Automatically generates a Clustered Index by default in SQL Server/MySQL. Automatically generates a Non-Clustered Index by default.

title: Write the SQL statement to create the table Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Salary, Dept_ID) with the following constraints: (i) Emp_ID is primary key, (ii) Email is unique and cannot be null, (iii) Salary must be at least 15000, and (iv) Dept_ID refers to Department(Dept_ID).
chunks: SQL DDL table creation with all specified constraints: CREATE TABLE Employee ( Emp_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE, Salary DECIMAL(10, 2) CHECK (Salary >= 15000), Dept_ID INT, CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID) ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE ); This statement enforces entity integrity on Emp_ID , unique identifier integrity on Email , business domain rules on Salary , and referential integrity linked to Department .

title: For the table PRODUCT_MAST(Product_ID, Product_Name, Price), write queries using (i) the LIKE operator to find products containing 'Pro' anywhere in the name, (ii) the BETWEEN operator to find products priced between 500 and 2000, and (iii) the IN operator to find products with specific IDs 10, 20 and 30.

title: Consider the tables Orders(Order_ID, Item_ID, Qty) and Inventory(Item_ID, Stock). Write an AFTER INSERT trigger on Orders that decrements the Stock in Inventory by Qty for the newly ordered item.
chunks: AFTER INSERT trigger in MySQL / standard SQL: DELIMITER $$ CREATE TRIGGER after_order_insert_decrement_stock AFTER INSERT ON Orders FOR EACH ROW BEGIN UPDATE Inventory SET Stock = Stock - NEW.Qty WHERE Item_ID = NEW.Item_ID; END $$ DELIMITER ; Explanation: AFTER INSERT : Fires immediately after a new order record is committed to Orders . FOR EACH ROW : Executes as a row-level trigger for every inserted tuple. NEW.Qty and NEW.Item_ID : References the newly inserted values from the Orders table to update the corresponding inventory item.

title: Given Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Basic_Salary, HRA, DA), write a stored procedure Calculate_Gross_Salary that computes Gross = Basic + HRA + DA for a given Emp_ID and returns it in an OUT parameter.
chunks: Stored procedure implementation in MySQL: DELIMITER $$ CREATE PROCEDURE Calculate_Gross_Salary( IN p_emp_id INT, OUT p_gross DECIMAL(10, 2) ) BEGIN SELECT (Basic_Salary + HRA + DA) INTO p_gross FROM Employee WHERE Emp_ID = p_emp_id; END $$ DELIMITER ; Calling the Stored Procedure: CALL Calculate_Gross_Salary(101, @gross_sal); SELECT @gross_sal AS Calculated_Gross;

title: Explain the set operations UNION, INTERSECT and MINUS/EXCEPT with an example on two tables A(val) = {1, 2, 3} and B(val) = {2, 3, 4}.
chunks: Given: $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{2, 3, 4\}$. UNION : Combines all distinct values from both tables, eliminating duplicates. SELECT val FROM A UNION SELECT val FROM B; Output: {1, 2, 3, 4} INTERSECT : Returns only the common values present in both tables. SELECT val FROM A INTERSECT SELECT val FROM B; Output: {2, 3} MINUS (or EXCEPT ): Returns values present in the first table that do not appear in the second table. SELECT val FROM A EXCEPT SELECT val FROM B; -- (A - B) Output: {1}

title: What is a stored procedure? Explain it with a short example.
chunks: A Stored Procedure is a precompiled collection of SQL statements and procedural logic (loops, if-else conditions, variables) stored directly on the database server under a designated name. Key Advantages: Reduced Network Traffic: A single CALL invokes complex multi-statement routines on the server. Performance: Parsed and compiled once; cached execution plans are reused. Security: Grants procedural execution rights without giving direct access to underlying base tables. Example: DELIMITER $$ CREATE PROCEDURE Update_Bonus(IN p_dept VARCHAR(20), IN p_bonus DECIMAL(10,2)) BEGIN UPDATE Employee SET Salary = Salary + p_bonus WHERE Dept = p_dept; END $$ DELIMITER ; -- Execution: CALL Update_Bonus('Sales', 5000);

title: Given the table STUDENT(Student_ID, First_Name, Last_Name, Email, Admission_Date), write queries to (i) display the full name as 'First_Name Last_Name', (ii) extract the year from Admission_Date, and (iii) replace the domain 'gmail.com' with 'univ.edu' in the Email column.
chunks: SQL queries utilizing string and date functions: (i) Display Full Name: SELECT CONCAT(First_Name, ' ', Last_Name) AS Full_Name FROM STUDENT; (ii) Extract Year from Admission_Date: SELECT Student_ID, YEAR(Admission_Date) AS Admission_Year FROM STUDENT; (iii) Replace 'gmail.com' with 'univ.edu': SELECT Student_ID, REPLACE(Email, 'gmail.com', 'univ.edu') AS University_Email FROM STUDENT;

title: Given the table ACCOUNT(Acc_No, Name, Balance, Nominee_Name), write queries that demonstrate handling NULL values: (i) find accounts with no nominee listed, (ii) display Nominee_Name or 'Not Assigned' if null using COALESCE, and (iii) show why 'Balance = NULL' is invalid and what should be used instead.
chunks: Handling NULL values in SQL: (i) Accounts with no nominee listed: SELECT Acc_No, Name FROM ACCOUNT WHERE Nominee_Name IS NULL; (ii) Display 'Not Assigned' if null using COALESCE: SELECT Acc_No, Name, COALESCE(Nominee_Name, 'Not Assigned') AS Nominee_Display FROM ACCOUNT; (iii) Why 'Balance = NULL' is invalid: In SQL's three-valued logic (3VL), NULL represents unknown/missing data, not a concrete value. Comparing anything to NULL using equality ( Balance = NULL ) evaluates to UNKNOWN (never TRUE ), so the query will always return zero rows . The correct syntax is IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL ): -- CORRECT: SELECT * FROM ACCOUNT WHERE Balance IS NULL;
