title: Name the four operations performed on an explicit cursor. Write a PL/SQL block that uses a cursor to print the names of all employees from Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Salary).
chunks: The four lifecycle operations of an explicit cursor in PL/SQL: DECLARE: Identifies and names the cursor, associating it with a specific SELECT query. OPEN: Executes the query, allocates private work memory, and positions the cursor pointer before the first row. FETCH: Retrieves the current active row into program variables and advances the pointer. CLOSE: Releases the active result set memory resources. PL/SQL Implementation: DECLARE v_name Employee.Name%TYPE; CURSOR emp_cursor IS SELECT Name FROM Employee; BEGIN OPEN emp_cursor; LOOP FETCH emp_cursor INTO v_name; EXIT WHEN emp_cursor%NOTFOUND; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Employee Name: ' || v_name); END LOOP; CLOSE emp_cursor; END;

title: Explain exception handling in PL/SQL. Differentiate between predefined and user-defined exceptions with an example.
chunks: Exception Handling in PL/SQL: An exception is a runtime error or unexpected event during code execution. The EXCEPTION block intercepts errors gracefully, preventing abnormal program crashes. Predefined vs. User-Defined Exceptions: Feature Predefined Exception User-Defined Exception Declaration Internally declared by Oracle/PL/SQL engine; names are standard keywords. Must be declared explicitly in the DECLARE section by the developer. Raising Raised automatically by the runtime engine when an internal error occurs (e.g., divide by zero). Raised explicitly by the programmer using the RAISE statement based on business rules. Example Names NO_DATA_FOUND , TOO_MANY_ROWS , ZERO_DIVIDE . e_insufficient_balance EXCEPTION; DECLARE v_bal NUMBER := 500; e_low_balance EXCEPTION; BEGIN IF v_bal < 1000 THEN RAISE e_low_balance; END IF; EXCEPTION WHEN e_low_balance THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Error: Minimum balance rule violated.'); WHEN OTHERS THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('An unexpected error occurred.'); END;

title: Write the output of each of the following MySQL statements: (i) SELECT UPPER('dbms') AS res;, (ii) SELECT MOD(17, 5) AS res;, (iii) SELECT SUBSTR('Database', 1, 4) AS res;, (iv) SELECT ROUND(45.678, 2) AS res;, (v) SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'Hello', 'World') AS res;, (vi) SELECT LENGTH('SQL') AS res;.
chunks: Outputs for each MySQL statement: SELECT UPPER('dbms'); Output: 'DBMS' (Converts lowercase letters to uppercase). SELECT MOD(17, 5); Output: 2 (Returns the remainder of $17 \div 5$, since $17 = 3 \times 5 + 2$). SELECT SUBSTR('Database', 1, 4); Output: 'Data' (Extracts 4 characters starting at position 1). SELECT ROUND(45.678, 2); Output: 45.68 (Rounds to 2 decimal places; 8 rounds up 7 to 8). SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'Hello', 'World'); Output: 'Hello' (Returns the first non-null argument in the parameter list). SELECT LENGTH('SQL'); Output: 3 (Returns character count length).

title: For the table ACCOUNT(Acc_No, Name, Balance), write a stored procedure (MySQL or PL/SQL) Transfer_Funds(from_acc, to_acc, amount) that transfers amount between accounts, verifying that from_acc has sufficient balance, and using transaction commands COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
chunks: Stored procedure implementing transactional fund transfer with balance checks in MySQL: DELIMITER $$ CREATE PROCEDURE Transfer_Funds( IN p_from_acc INT, IN p_to_acc INT, IN p_amount DECIMAL(12, 2) ) proc_body: BEGIN DECLARE v_from_balance DECIMAL(12, 2); DECLARE v_to_exists INT DEFAULT 0; -- Error handler to automatically rollback on any SQL error DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION BEGIN ROLLBACK; SELECT 'Transaction Failed: System Error encountered. Rolled back.' AS Result; END; -- Start explicit transaction START TRANSACTION; -- 1. Check sender balance with row lock (FOR UPDATE) SELECT Balance INTO v_from_balance FROM ACCOUNT WHERE Acc_No = p_from_acc FOR UPDATE; IF v_from_balance IS NULL THEN ROLLBACK; SELECT 'Transfer Failed: Source account does not exist.' AS Result; LEAVE proc_body; END IF; IF v_from_balance < p_amount THEN ROLLBACK; SELECT 'Transfer Failed: Insufficient funds in source account.' AS Result; LEAVE proc_body; END IF; -- 2. Check destination account existence SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_to_exists FROM ACCOUNT WHERE Acc_No = p_to_acc; IF v_to_exists = 0 THEN ROLLBACK; SELECT 'Transfer Failed: Destination account does not exist.' AS Result; LEAVE proc_body; END IF; -- 3. Execute transfer UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - p_amount WHERE Acc_No = p_from_acc; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + p_amount WHERE Acc_No = p_to_acc; -- Commit atomic transfer COMMIT; SELECT 'Transfer Successful: Funds transferred and committed.' AS Result; END $$ DELIMITER ;

title: Given Student(Roll_No, Name, Marks) and Student_Audit(Audit_ID, Roll_No, Old_Marks, New_Marks, Change_Date, Changed_By), write an AFTER UPDATE trigger on Student that records any change in Marks into Student_Audit, including the user and timestamp.
chunks: 1. Create the Audit Table: CREATE TABLE Student_Audit ( Audit_ID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, Roll_No INT, Old_Marks DECIMAL(5, 2), New_Marks DECIMAL(5, 2), Change_Date TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, Changed_By VARCHAR(100) ); 2. AFTER UPDATE Trigger on Student: DELIMITER $$ CREATE TRIGGER after_student_marks_update AFTER UPDATE ON Student FOR EACH ROW BEGIN -- Fire audit record only if marks actually changed IF OLD.Marks <> NEW.Marks OR (OLD.Marks IS NULL AND NEW.Marks IS NOT NULL) THEN INSERT INTO Student_Audit ( Roll_No, Old_Marks, New_Marks, Change_Date, Changed_By ) VALUES ( OLD.Roll_No, OLD.Marks, NEW.Marks, NOW(), USER() -- Built-in SQL function returning active username ); END IF; END $$ DELIMITER ; Explanation: Compares OLD.Marks with NEW.Marks . If modified, logs the previous mark, new mark, current system timestamp ( NOW() ), and operating session user ( USER() ) into the audit trail.

title: Write the CREATE TABLE statement for Orders(Order_ID, Cust_ID, Amount, Status, Order_Date) with: (i) Order_ID as primary key, (ii) Amount must be strictly positive, (iii) Status can only be 'Pending', 'Shipped', or 'Delivered', and (iv) Order_Date defaults to the current date. Then explain what ON DELETE CASCADE would do on this table.
chunks: 1. CREATE TABLE Statement with Constraints: CREATE TABLE Orders ( Order_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Cust_ID INT NOT NULL, Amount DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (Amount > 0), Status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (Status IN ('Pending', 'Shipped', 'Delivered')), Order_Date DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE), CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (Cust_ID) REFERENCES Customer(Cust_ID) ON DELETE CASCADE ); 2. Explanation of ON DELETE CASCADE : When defined on the foreign key referencing the Customer table, ON DELETE CASCADE dictates that if a customer record is deleted from the parent Customer table, the database management system will automatically delete all associated order rows for that customer in the Orders table. Benefit: Prevents dangling child references and eliminates manual cascading deletion code in applications. Caution: Must be used carefully in commercial finance systems where historical accounting/invoicing records must be retained even if customer accounts are deactivated.

title: Give the output of each of the following MySQL statements and justify your answer: (i) SELECT NULL = NULL;, (ii) SELECT NULL <=> NULL;, (iii) SELECT 5 + NULL;, (iv) SELECT CONCAT('Hello', NULL);, and (v) SELECT COUNT(comm) FROM (SELECT NULL AS comm UNION ALL SELECT 5) t;.
chunks: Outputs and theoretical justifications: SELECT NULL = NULL; Output: NULL Justification: In standard SQL, NULL represents unknown/missing information. Two unknown values cannot be asserted to be equal; the comparison evaluates to UNKNOWN , displayed as NULL . SELECT NULL <=> NULL; Output: 1 (TRUE) Justification: The spaceship operator ( <=> ) is MySQL's NULL-safe equality operator . It treats two NULL values as equal, returning 1 . SELECT 5 + NULL; Output: NULL Justification: Any arithmetic operation involving NULL yields NULL because operating on an unknown quantity produces an unknown result. SELECT CONCAT('Hello', NULL); Output: NULL Justification: In MySQL, CONCAT() returns NULL if any of its arguments is NULL (unlike CONCAT_WS() ). SELECT COUNT(comm) FROM (SELECT NULL AS comm UNION ALL SELECT 5) t; Output: 1 Justification: COUNT(column_name) counts only non-null values. Out of the 2 rows (NULL and 5), only row 5 is non-null, yielding a count of 1.

title: A bank has four requirements: (i) automatically log every change made to an account's balance, (ii) sequentially generate new account numbers, (iii) iterate through all dormant accounts and send alerts, and (iv) provide a routine to deposit money into an account. Say which of trigger, cursor, AUTO_INCREMENT or stored procedure should be used for each requirement, with reasons, and write the code for (i) and (iii).
chunks: Architectural Component Selection: (i) Automatically log balance changes: TRIGGER (AFTER UPDATE) , because logging must fire automatically without relying on application code. (ii) Sequentially generate account numbers: AUTO_INCREMENT / SEQUENCE , designed specifically for monotonic unique key generation. (iii) Iterate through dormant accounts: CURSOR in a PL/SQL block , designed for row-by-row programmatic traversal. (iv) Deposit money routine: STORED PROCEDURE , encapsulates transactional business logic callable on demand. Code Implementation for (i) Audit Trigger: CREATE TRIGGER audit_account_balance AFTER UPDATE ON Account FOR EACH ROW BEGIN IF OLD.Balance <> NEW.Balance THEN INSERT INTO Account_Log(Acc_No, Old_Bal, New_Bal, Mod_Time) VALUES (OLD.Acc_No, OLD.Balance, NEW.Balance, NOW()); END IF; END; Code Implementation for (iii) Dormant Account Cursor: DECLARE v_acc_no Account.Acc_No%TYPE; CURSOR dormant_cur IS SELECT Acc_No FROM Account WHERE Last_Active < CURRENT_DATE - 365; BEGIN OPEN dormant_cur; LOOP FETCH dormant_cur INTO v_acc_no; EXIT WHEN dormant_cur%NOTFOUND; Send_Alert(v_acc_no); -- External alerting procedure END LOOP; CLOSE dormant_cur; END;

title: The table Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Salary, Dept_ID) already holds data in which some Email values are NULL and some are duplicated. The DBA wants to add NOT NULL and UNIQUE constraints on Email, a CHECK constraint (Salary > 0) and a foreign key on Dept_ID referring to Department(Dept_ID). Write the ALTER TABLE statements, analyse which of them may fail on the existing data and why, and describe how the data should be corrected beforehand.
chunks: 1. ALTER TABLE Statements: -- A. Add NOT NULL on Email ALTER TABLE Employee MODIFY Email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL; -- B. Add UNIQUE on Email ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT uq_emp_email UNIQUE (Email); -- C. Add CHECK on Salary ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (Salary > 0); -- D. Add FOREIGN KEY on Dept_ID ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID); 2. Failure Analysis on Existing Data: Statement A (NOT NULL) will FAIL: Existing rows contain NULL in Email . Modifying a column to NOT NULL is immediately aborted by the engine upon detecting existing NULLs. Statement B (UNIQUE) will FAIL: Existing duplicate email addresses violate the uniqueness condition. Statement D (FOREIGN KEY) may FAIL: If any existing Dept_ID in Employee does not exist in Department (orphaned rows), foreign key creation will fail. 3. Prior Data Rectification Steps: Fix NULL Emails: Update NULL emails with unique placeholder addresses: UPDATE Employee SET Email = CONCAT('emp_', Emp_ID, '@company.com') WHERE Email IS NULL; Fix Duplicate Emails: Identify duplicates and update or remove redundant copies. Fix Orphaned Dept_IDs: Set invalid Dept_ID values to NULL or insert missing parent departments.

title: (i) Write a stored function percent_to_grade(p) that returns 'A' for 75 and above, 'B' for 60 or more but below 75, 'C' for 40 or more but below 60, and 'F' for below 40. (ii) Show how this function can be called in a SELECT query on Student(Roll_No, Name, Marks, Total_Marks) to display each student's grade.
chunks: (i) Stored Function Definition in MySQL: DELIMITER $$ CREATE FUNCTION percent_to_grade(p DECIMAL(5, 2)) RETURNS CHAR(1) DETERMINISTIC BEGIN DECLARE v_grade CHAR(1); IF p >= 75.0 THEN SET v_grade = 'A'; ELSEIF p >= 60.0 THEN SET v_grade = 'B'; ELSEIF p >= 40.0 THEN SET v_grade = 'C'; ELSE SET v_grade = 'F'; END IF; RETURN v_grade; END $$ DELIMITER ; (ii) Calling the Stored Function in a SELECT Query: SELECT Roll_No, Name, Marks, Total_Marks, ROUND((Marks / Total_Marks) * 100, 2) AS Percentage, percent_to_grade((Marks / Total_Marks) * 100) AS Grade FROM Student; The function executes inline on every retrieved record, transforming computed percentages directly into letter grades.

title: Consider Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Department, Salary) and Employee_Archive(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Department, Salary, Deletion_Date). Write a BEFORE DELETE trigger on Employee that archives every deleted employee record into Employee_Archive with the current date.
chunks: 1. Archive Table Definition: CREATE TABLE Employee_Archive ( Emp_ID INT, Emp_Name VARCHAR(100), Department VARCHAR(50), Salary DECIMAL(10, 2), Deletion_Date TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); 2. BEFORE DELETE Trigger Implementation: DELIMITER $$ CREATE TRIGGER before_employee_delete_archive BEFORE DELETE ON Employee FOR EACH ROW BEGIN INSERT INTO Employee_Archive ( Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Department, Salary, Deletion_Date ) VALUES ( OLD.Emp_ID, OLD.Emp_Name, OLD.Department, OLD.Salary, NOW() ); END $$ DELIMITER ; Explanation: BEFORE DELETE ensures the record's details are safely archived prior to disk deletion. The OLD qualifier captures attribute values of the row undergoing deletion. If the deletion later rolls back, the archive insert is rolled back as well, preserving transactional consistency.

title: Write a stored procedure (MySQL or PL/SQL) that accepts a number n and (i) uses a WHILE loop to compute and return the factorial of n, and (ii) handles the case where n < 0 by returning -1.
chunks: Factorial stored procedure implementation in MySQL: DELIMITER $$ CREATE PROCEDURE Compute_Factorial( IN p_n INT, OUT p_fact BIGINT ) BEGIN DECLARE v_counter INT; -- Case (ii): Handle negative inputs IF p_n < 0 THEN SET p_fact = -1; ELSEIF p_n = 0 OR p_n = 1 THEN SET p_fact = 1; ELSE SET p_fact = 1; SET v_counter = 1; -- Case (i): WHILE loop to compute factorial WHILE v_counter <= p_n DO SET p_fact = p_fact * v_counter; SET v_counter = v_counter + 1; END WHILE; END IF; END $$ DELIMITER ; Execution Demonstration: CALL Compute_Factorial(5, @res); SELECT @res; -- Returns 120 CALL Compute_Factorial(-3, @res); SELECT @res; -- Returns -1

title: Consider the tables Product(Prod_ID, Prod_Name, Stock), Orders(Order_ID, Prod_ID, Qty) and Out_Of_Stock_Log(Log_ID, Prod_ID, Log_Time). Write an AFTER INSERT trigger on Orders that updates the Stock in Product and, if the Stock falls to zero or below, inserts a record into Out_Of_Stock_Log.
chunks: Trigger with stock update and threshold alerting: DELIMITER $$ CREATE TRIGGER after_order_stock_and_alert AFTER INSERT ON Orders FOR EACH ROW BEGIN DECLARE v_current_stock INT; -- 1. Deduct ordered quantity from Product stock UPDATE Product SET Stock = Stock - NEW.Qty WHERE Prod_ID = NEW.Prod_ID; -- 2. Fetch updated stock level SELECT Stock INTO v_current_stock FROM Product WHERE Prod_ID = NEW.Prod_ID; -- 3. If stock drops to zero or below, record in Out_Of_Stock_Log IF v_current_stock <= 0 THEN INSERT INTO Out_Of_Stock_Log (Prod_ID, Log_Time) VALUES (NEW.Prod_ID, NOW()); END IF; END $$ DELIMITER ; Operational Flow: Order inserted $\rightarrow$ triggers execution. Stock decremented by NEW.Qty . Stock checked: if $\le 0$, automatically generates alert entry in Out_Of_Stock_Log .

title: Analyse the following MySQL transaction on the table Dept(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), which is initially empty: START TRANSACTION; INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (1, 'HR'); SAVEPOINT sp1; INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (2, 'Finance'); SAVEPOINT sp2; INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (3, 'Marketing'); ROLLBACK TO sp1; INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (4, 'Operations'); COMMIT; State the final contents of Dept with reasons, and explain the purpose of SAVEPOINT.
chunks: 1. Step-by-Step Transaction Execution Trace: Step Operation Current Transaction State 1 START TRANSACTION; New transaction begins. Table is empty. 2 INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (1, 'HR'); Row (1, 'HR') inserted. 3 SAVEPOINT sp1; Marker sp1 established (contains {(1, 'HR')} ). 4 INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (2, 'Finance'); Row (2, 'Finance') inserted. 5 SAVEPOINT sp2; Marker sp2 established. 6 INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (3, 'Marketing'); Row (3, 'Marketing') inserted. 7 ROLLBACK TO sp1; All operations after sp1 are undone! Rows (2, 'Finance') and (3, 'Marketing') are rolled back. Table reverts to {(1, 'HR')} . 8 INSERT INTO Dept VALUES (4, 'Operations'); Row (4, 'Operations') inserted. 9 COMMIT; All active changes are permanently saved to disk. 2. Final Contents of Dept : Dept_ID Dept_Name 1 HR 4 Operations 3. Purpose of SAVEPOINT: A SAVEPOINT creates intermediate checkpoint markers within a transaction. It allows the application to perform partial rollbacks to a specific point without discarding the entire transaction, enabling resilient error recovery in complex multi-step database procedures.

title: Define a transaction. Mention the two ways in which a transaction can terminate.
chunks: A transaction is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more operations (such as read, write, or update). It executes as an indivisible unit to preserve database consistency. A transaction terminates in two ways: Commit: The transaction completes successfully, making all its modifications permanent and durable on disk. Abort (Rollback): The transaction terminates abnormally; all partial changes are undone, returning the database to its pre-transaction state.

title: Three transactions are running such that T1 waits for a lock held by T2, T2 waits for a lock held by T3, and T3 waits for a lock held by T1. Draw the wait-for graph and state whether a deadlock exists.
chunks: A Wait-For Graph (WFG) is a directed graph where vertices represent active transactions and directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ is waiting for a lock held by $T_j$. Deadlock Status: Yes, a deadlock exists . The wait-for graph contains the directed cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3 \to T_1$. In concurrency control, a directed cycle in a WFG is a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock.

title: What is meant by a recoverable schedule?
chunks: A schedule $S$ is recoverable if, for every pair of transactions $T_i$ and $T_j$ where $T_j$ reads a data item previously written by $T_i$, the commit operation of $T_i$ precedes the commit operation of $T_j$ ($Commit(T_i) < Commit(T_j)$). Significance: Prevents dirty read commits. If $T_i$ aborts, $T_j$ can also be safely rolled back because it has not yet committed. Database Invariant: Commercial DBMSs mandate recoverable schedules to guarantee atomicity and durability during crashes.

title: Define deadlock and state any two conditions that are necessary for it to occur.
chunks: A deadlock is an execution state where two or more concurrent transactions are permanently blocked because each holds a lock on a data item that another requires, and none can proceed without releasing locks. Two necessary conditions for deadlock are: Mutual Exclusion: A resource is held in an exclusive, non-shareable mode (such as an $X$-lock). Hold and Wait: A transaction holds granted resources while requesting additional resources held by other transactions.

title: What is a checkpoint in a DBMS? State its purpose in recovery.
chunks: A checkpoint is a synchronization record written to the log during normal operation after flushing all modified buffer blocks (dirty pages) from volatile memory to stable disk storage. Purpose in recovery: Bounds Log Scan: Limits how far back the recovery manager must scan the log during crash restart, eliminating the need to process the log from the very beginning. Reduces Redo Work: Transactions committed prior to the checkpoint already have their updates safely on disk, significantly shortening system recovery downtime.

title: Differentiate between clustered and non-clustered indexes.
chunks: The key differences between clustered and non-clustered indexes are: Physical Ordering: A clustered index dictates the physical sorting order of actual table rows on disk (only one clustered index per table). A non-clustered index maintains an independent logical order without rearranging physical rows. Leaf Node Content: Leaf nodes of a clustered index contain the actual data records. In a non-clustered index, leaf nodes contain index keys and row pointers (RID / primary key) to data records.

title: What is a fact table and a dimension table in a data warehouse?
chunks: In data warehouse dimensional modeling (e.g., star schema): Fact Table: The central table containing quantitative numerical measurements (metrics) of a business process (e.g., units_sold , total_amount ) along with foreign keys referencing related dimension tables. Dimension Table: Surrounding companion tables containing descriptive contextual attributes (e.g., customer names, store locations, calendar quarters) used for filtering, grouping, and slicing analytical queries.

title: Draw the state diagram of a transaction and explain each of its states.
chunks: During its lifecycle, a database transaction progresses through several distinct execution states to guarantee ACID properties and system consistency: Active: The initial execution state where the transaction begins and executes its read and write database operations. Partially Committed: Entered immediately after the final statement has executed, but updates still reside in memory buffers and have not yet been flushed to stable disk storage. Failed: Entered when normal execution cannot proceed due to hardware failures, logical errors, or concurrency violations. Aborted: The transaction is rolled back, all dirty updates are undone, and the database is restored to its pre-transaction state. The transaction can either restart or terminate. Committed: Entered when all log records and updates are permanently recorded on stable storage, guaranteeing durability.

title: Explain consistent and inconsistent states of a database using the example of a money transfer between two bank accounts that fails midway.
chunks: A consistent state satisfies all integrity constraints and business rules, while an inconsistent state violates these rules due to partial execution or unhandled failures. Bank Transfer Scenario: Consider transferring ₹1,000 from Account $A$ (initial balance ₹5,000) to Account $B$ (initial balance ₹3,000). The database consistency invariant requires that total balance $A + B = ₹8,000$. Midway Failure: The transaction executes A = A - 1000 ($A$ becomes ₹4,000). Before B = B + 1000 can execute, the system crashes. Inconsistent State: If left unrecovered, $A + B = ₹4,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹7,000$. ₹1,000 has vanished, creating an inconsistent state. Recovery to Consistent State: The recovery manager rolls back $A$ to ₹5,000 via transaction undo logs, re-establishing the invariant $A + B = ₹8,000$.

title: List the different types of failures in a database system and explain how recovery from a transaction failure is carried out.
chunks: Database systems are subject to three fundamental classes of failures: Transaction Failure: Internal logical errors (e.g., divide by zero, bad input) or system errors (e.g., deadlock abort, buffer overflow). System Crash: Hardware malfunctions or operating system crashes causing volatile main memory contents to be lost without corrupting non-volatile disk storage. Disk Failure: Head crashes or bad disk sectors destroying physical storage blocks. Recovery from Transaction Failure: When a transaction fails, the recovery manager performs an UNDO operation using the transaction log. It scans the log backwards, extracts the old values (before-images) of all modified data items, writes these original values back to the database, and appends an <abort T> log record.

title: Explain the lost update and dirty read problems that arise when transactions execute concurrently, with an example of each.
chunks: Concurrency anomalies occur when transactions interleave without adequate synchronization: Lost Update (Write-Write Conflict): Occurs when two transactions read the same data item and subsequently update it based on the earlier read value. The second write overwrites and obliterates the first write without incorporating its modifications. Example: Account balance is ₹100. $T_1$ reads 100 and computes 150. Concurrently, $T_2$ reads 100 and computes 120. $T_1$ writes 150, then $T_2$ writes 120. $T_1$'s ₹50 deposit is completely lost. Dirty Read (Read-Write Conflict): Occurs when transaction $T_2$ reads a data item modified by transaction $T_1$ that has not yet committed. If $T_1$ subsequently aborts, $T_2$ has acted on transient, invalid data. Example: $T_1$ updates balance from ₹100 to ₹500. $T_2$ reads ₹500 and approves a purchase. $T_1$ aborts and rolls back to ₹100. $T_2$'s read was 'dirty'.

title: Distinguish between conflict serializability and view serializability with an example.
chunks: Serializability guarantees that concurrent schedules produce results identical to some serial execution: Conflict Serializability: A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting concurrent operations. This holds if and only if its precedence (conflict) graph is acyclic. Tested efficiently in polynomial time $O(V + E)$. View Serializability: A weaker, broader condition requiring identical initial reads, dependent reads, and final writes as some serial schedule. Testing view serializability is NP-complete. Example: Consider schedule $S: R_1(A), W_2(A), W_1(A), W_3(A)$. Here, operations conflict in both directions ($T_1 \to T_2$ and $T_2 \to T_1$), producing a cycle in the precedence graph; thus $S$ is not conflict serializable . However, due to blind writes ($W_3(A)$ overwriting $A$), $S$ produces the exact same view as serial schedule $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3$, making it view serializable .

title: Explain the role of the concurrency control manager and the lock manager, and describe how the lock table is used to grant or queue lock requests.
chunks: The concurrency control manager ensures serializability, isolation, and consistency across interleaved transactions. It delegates resource locking to the lock manager . The lock manager maintains an in-memory hash table called the lock table , indexed by data item ID: Granted List: Holds records of transactions currently granted a lock on the item, along with lock mode (Shared $S$ or Exclusive $X$). Wait Queue: When a transaction requests an incompatible lock (e.g., $X$-lock while an $S$-lock is held), the request cannot be granted. The lock manager suspends the transaction and appends it to the item's FIFO wait queue. Release & Grant: When a lock holder unlocks the item, the lock manager inspects the wait queue, awakens compatible waiting transactions, and updates the granted list.

title: Explain the role of TCL commands in controlling transactions.
chunks: Transaction Control Language (TCL) commands manage database transactions to ensure data integrity and ACID properties: COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made by the transaction to disk. Locks are released, and modifications become visible to other concurrent users. ROLLBACK: Reverts all modifications made by an uncommitted transaction, returning the database to the state prior to transaction initiation or to a specified savepoint. SAVEPOINT: Establishes intermediate checkpoints within a transaction. Allows partial rollback (e.g., ROLLBACK TO sp1 ) without undoing the entire transaction. SET TRANSACTION: Configures isolation levels (e.g., READ COMMITTED , SERIALIZABLE ) and access modes ( READ ONLY vs READ WRITE ) before operations begin.

title: With an example, explain the ACID properties of a transaction.
chunks: ACID properties guarantee reliable database transactions. Consider transferring ₹1,000 from account $A$ to account $B$: Atomicity: All operations succeed or none do. Either both debiting $A$ and crediting $B$ succeed, or the transaction aborts and leaves both balances unchanged. Consistency: The transaction transforms the database from one valid state to another, preserving integrity invariants (e.g., total funds $A + B$ remains constant before and after). Isolation: Intermediate states are hidden from concurrent transactions. Another transaction reading $A$ and $B$ cannot see $A$ deducted before $B$ is credited. Durability: Once committed, updates persist permanently on non-volatile storage, even if a power failure or system crash occurs immediately afterward.

title: Consider the schedule S: R1(A), W1(A), R2(A), W2(A), R1(B), W1(B), R2(B), W2(B), where Ri and Wi denote the read and write operations of transaction Ti. Draw the precedence graph of S, determine whether S is conflict serializable and, if so, give an equivalent serial schedule.
chunks: To analyze schedule $S$, we identify all pairs of conflicting operations (operations by different transactions on the same data item where at least one is a write): Conflicts on Data Item A: $R_1(A) < W_2(A)$, $W_1(A) < R_2(A)$, and $W_1(A) < W_2(A)$ all establish precedence edge $T_1 \to T_2$. Conflicts on Data Item B: $R_1(B) < W_2(B)$, $W_1(B) < R_2(B)$, and $W_1(B) < W_2(B)$ also establish edge $T_1 \to T_2$. Graph Analysis: In a precedence graph, a directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ executes a conflicting operation before $T_j$. Here, all conflicting pairs direct from $T_1$ to $T_2$ with zero reverse edges. Serializability: Because the precedence graph contains no directed cycles (strictly acyclic), schedule $S$ is conflict serializable . Equivalent Serial Schedule: Topological ordering gives $\langle T_1, T_2 \rangle$ ($T_1$ followed by $T_2$).

title: Explain log-based recovery with the deferred database modification and immediate database modification techniques.
chunks: Log-based recovery uses a write-ahead log (WAL) on stable storage to restore database consistency after crashes: Deferred Database Modification: All write operations update only the log buffer in memory; the actual database on disk is modified only after the transaction commits. Recovery Policy: Since uncommitted updates are never written to disk, an UNDO is never required (NO-UNDO/REDO algorithm). During crash recovery, the DBMS only REDOes transactions whose log contains both <T start> and <T commit> . Immediate Database Modification: Database updates can be written to disk while the transaction is still active, before committing (following WAL rules). Recovery Policy: Requires both UNDO and REDO (UNDO/REDO algorithm). Uncommitted transactions that modified disk blocks must be UNDONE, while committed transactions must be REDONE to guarantee durability.

title: Explain dense and sparse indexes with an example. Which of the two requires less storage space and why?
chunks: Indexes accelerate search key lookups by mapping keys to disk block locations: Dense Index: An index record appears for every search-key value in the data file. For duplicate keys, it points to the first record or a list of records. Fast lookups, but large index footprint. Example: An employee table with 10,000 records has 10,000 entries in its dense index. Sparse Index: An index record appears for only some search-key values (typically one anchor key per disk block). Requires data records to be physically sorted by search key. Example: 10,000 records stored across 100 blocks require only 100 entries in a sparse index. Storage Comparison: A sparse index requires significantly less storage space because it contains far fewer entries, allowing it to remain memory-resident and reducing I/O operations.

title: Explain the unrepeatable read and phantom read problems of concurrent transactions with an example for each.
chunks: These two read anomalies occur under relaxed SQL isolation levels: Unrepeatable (Fuzzy) Read: Transaction $T_1$ reads a specific row. Concurrently, transaction $T_2$ modifies or deletes that row and commits. When $T_1$ re-reads the exact same row, it discovers that the values have changed or the row disappeared. Example: $T_1$ reads employee John's salary as ₹50,000. $T_2$ updates John's salary to ₹60,000 and commits. $T_1$ re-reads John's record and finds ₹60,000, violating read repeatability. Phantom Read: Transaction $T_1$ reads a set of rows satisfying a search predicate. Concurrently, transaction $T_2$ inserts a new row matching that predicate and commits. When $T_1$ re-executes the query, a new 'phantom' row appears. Example: $T_1$ runs SELECT count(*) WHERE dept='IT' (gets 5). $T_2$ inserts a new IT employee and commits. $T_1$ re-runs the count and gets 6.

title: Distinguish between serial and non-serial schedules. Define conflict serializability and explain why a DBMS needs serializable schedules.
chunks: A schedule defines the chronological execution sequence of operations across concurrent transactions. 1. Serial vs. Non-Serial Schedules: Feature Serial Schedule Non-Serial (Interleaved) Schedule Execution Order Operations of each transaction execute consecutively without interleaving. Operations of multiple transactions interleave concurrently. Throughput & CPU Poor CPU and I/O resource utilization; waiting transactions block everything. High throughput and optimal resource utilization during I/O stalls. Consistency Always preserves consistency automatically without concurrency control. Can lead to anomalies (lost updates, dirty reads) unless serialized. Response Time High turnaround time for long transactions. Significantly reduced latency for short transactions. 2. Conflict Serializability: A non-serial schedule $S$ is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into an equivalent serial schedule by a sequence of swaps of non-conflicting adjacent operations. Two operations conflict if they are issued by different transactions, operate on the same data item, and at least one is a write operation ($R_i(X)-W_j(X)$, $W_i(X)-R_j(X)$, or $W_i(X)-W_j(X)$). A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph (conflict graph) contains no directed cycles. 3. Why a DBMS Needs Serializable Schedules: Guaranteed Correctness: Since any serial execution preserves database consistency, a serializable concurrent schedule guarantees that the final state is mathematically correct. Concurrency without Inconsistency: Allows the DBMS to maximize hardware parallelism, multi-core CPU throughput, and disk I/O overlap while completely eliminating race conditions and isolation anomalies. ACID Isolation Invariant: Commercial database engines mandate serializability to fulfill the SQL standard Isolation requirement without forcing transactions to run strictly one at a time.

title: Explain recoverable, non-recoverable and cascadeless schedules and cascading rollback, giving a short example schedule for each.
chunks: Transaction recovery properties define how concurrent schedules behave when uncommitted dependencies encounter unexpected failures or aborts: 1. Non-Recoverable Schedule: Occurs when transaction $T_2$ reads a data item modified by uncommitted transaction $T_1$, and $T_2$ commits before $T_1$. If $T_1$ subsequently aborts, $T_2$ has committed dirty data that cannot be rolled back without violating the Durability property of ACID. Example: $S_1: W_1(A), R_2(A), Commit(T_2), Abort(T_1)$. Once $T_2$ commits, its results are permanently written to disk, leaving the database in an unrecoverable corrupted state. 2. Recoverable Schedule: A schedule is recoverable if, whenever transaction $T_2$ reads a data item written by transaction $T_1$, the commit operation of $T_1$ precedes the commit operation of $T_2$ ($Commit(T_1) < Commit(T_2)$). Example: $S_2: W_1(A), R_2(A), Commit(T_1), Commit(T_2)$. If $T_1$ aborts instead, $T_2$ has not yet committed and can be safely aborted too. 3. Cascading Rollback: A phenomenon where the failure and rollback of a single transaction triggers a chain reaction of aborts across multiple dependent, uncommitted transactions that read its dirty uncommitted updates. Example: $S_3: W_1(A), R_2(A), W_2(B), R_3(B), Abort(T_1)$. Because $T_1$ aborts, $T_2$ must abort, which in turn forces $T_3$ to abort, squandering significant CPU and disk I/O work. 4. Cascadeless Schedule: A schedule is

cascadeless (avoids cascading aborts) if every transaction reads only values written by already committed transactions ($Read_j(X)$ is delayed until after $Commit(T_i)$). Example: $S_4: W_1(A), Commit(T_1), R_2(A), Commit(T_2)$. Since $T_2$ only reads after $T_1$ commits, an abort of $T_1$ can never affect $T_2$. Every cascadeless schedule is strictly recoverable. Containment Hierarchy: The classes of schedules satisfy the strict inclusion relation: $\text{Strict Schedules} \subset \text{Cascadeless Schedules} \subset \text{Recoverable Schedules} \subset \text{All Possible Schedules}$. Commercial database engines enforce cascadelessness or strictness to maintain continuous system throughput.

title: Explain how deadlocks are detected using a wait-for graph, and explain the deadlock recovery schemes: victim selection, rollback and the avoidance of starvation.
chunks: A deadlock occurs in lock-based concurrency control when transactions enter circular wait states for held locks. 1. Deadlock Detection via Wait-For Graph (WFG): A Wait-For Graph is a directed graph $G = (V, E)$ maintained dynamically by the lock manager where vertices $V$ represent active transactions and directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ is suspended waiting for a lock currently held by $T_j$. When a lock request cannot be granted, an edge is added; when a lock is released, corresponding edges are deleted. The lock manager invokes cycle-detection algorithms (e.g., Depth-First Search or Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm) at scheduled intervals. A deadlock exists if and only if the WFG contains a directed cycle. 2. Deadlock Recovery Schemes: Victim Selection: When a cycle is detected, the DBMS chooses one transaction in the cycle to abort. The selection minimizes overall rollback overhead based on criteria such as elapsed execution time, remaining queries, number of modified rows, and number of cascading rollbacks prevented. Rollback Policy: Total Rollback: Abort the victim completely and restart it from the very beginning. Partial Rollback: Roll back the victim only to an intermediate savepoint sufficient to release the contested lock and break the graph cycle,

saving prior computational work. Avoidance of Starvation: If victim selection always chooses the youngest transaction or the one with the fewest updates, that transaction could repeatedly be aborted and starved from ever finishing. To prevent starvation, the DBMS associates an abort count with each transaction; each abort increments its priority so an older transaction is never starved indefinitely.

title: Explain shared (S) and exclusive (X) locks along with the lock compatibility matrix, and describe the basic two-phase locking protocol, including its growing phase, shrinking phase and lock point.
chunks: Lock-based concurrency control protocols restrict concurrent data access using complementary lock modes and acquisition phases: 1. Shared (S) and Exclusive (X) Locks: Shared Lock ($S$): Read-only lock mode. If a transaction holds a shared lock on data item $Q$, other concurrent transactions can also acquire shared locks on $Q$ ($S-S$ is compatible). No writes are permitted. Exclusive Lock ($X$): Read-write lock mode. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on $Q$ at any given moment ($X-S$ and $X-X$ are strictly incompatible). Lock Compatibility Matrix: Requested \ Held Shared ($S$) Exclusive ($X$) Shared ($S$) Compatible (True) Incompatible (False) Exclusive ($X$) Incompatible (False) Incompatible (False) 2. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol: The basic 2PL protocol guarantees conflict serializability by requiring every transaction to separate its lock operations into two distinct, non-overlapping phases: Phase 1: Growing (Expanding) Phase: The transaction acquires new locks as needed and may upgrade locks ($S \to X$). It cannot release any lock under any circumstances. Lock Point: The exact instant when the transaction acquires its final lock (reaches peak lock count). The chronological order of lock points across transactions dictates their exact conflict serialization order. Phase 2: Shrinking (Contracting) Phase: The transaction releases held locks and may downgrade locks ($X \to S$). It cannot acquire any new locks once this phase begins. Serializability Guarantee: Because transactions never acquire new locks after releasing an earlier lock, no circular data item dependencies can be created, proving that 2PL guarantees conflict serializability.

title: Compare strict and rigorous two-phase locking with the help of an example, and state the benefits of each.
chunks: Strict 2PL and Rigorous 2PL are specialized variants of the Two-Phase Locking protocol that enforce stronger guarantees than basic 2PL. 1. Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL): Rule: In addition to basic 2PL rules, a transaction must hold all its exclusive ($X$) locks until it terminates (commits or aborts). Shared ($S$) locks can be released during the shrinking phase before commit. Benefits: Guarantees recoverable and cascadeless schedules (prevents dirty reads), simplifying transaction rollback without cascading aborts. Allows concurrent reads to proceed earlier when shared locks are released. 2. Rigorous Two-Phase Locking (Rigorous 2PL): Rule: A transaction must hold all locks (both Shared $S$ and Exclusive $X$) until it terminates (commits or aborts). The shrinking phase collapses to the commit/abort point. Benefits: Guarantees strict serializability. Transactions can be serialized in the exact order in which they commit, making schedule analysis and replication coordination straightforward. 3. Comparative Example Schedule: Consider transaction $T_1$ needing to read $A$ and update $B$, and transaction $T_2$ needing to read $A$: Under Strict 2PL: $T_1$ acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. After reading $A$, $T_1$ can release $S(A)$ early. $T_2$ can immediately acquire $S(A)$ and read $A$ before $T_1$ commits. However, $T_1$ retains $X(B)$ until commit. Under Rigorous 2PL: $T_1$

acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. $T_1$ cannot release $S(A)$ until it commits. $T_2$ must wait if it needs an exclusive lock, ensuring strict chronological locking isolation. Dimension Strict 2PL Rigorous 2PL X-locks held until Commit / Abort Commit / Abort S-locks held until Can release in shrinking phase Commit / Abort Concurrency Level Higher (early S-lock release) Lower (locks held longer) Commit Ordering May differ from lock point Identical to commit order

title: Explain the architecture of a data warehouse (data sources, staging area, warehouse and presentation layer), describe the ETL process and state the role of data marts.
chunks: A Data Warehouse (DW) is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, and non-volatile collection of corporate data structured for management decision-support analysis. 1. Architectural Layers: Data Sources: Operational transactional databases (OLTP), enterprise ERP and CRM systems, flat log files, web clickstreams, and third-party APIs. Staging Area: An intermediate holding and processing area where incoming data is extracted, sanitized, validated, and normalized before warehouse insertion, isolating production OLTP systems from query load. Warehouse (Enterprise Storage): The central repository storing integrated historical and atomic granular data organized according to enterprise-wide relational or dimensional data models. Presentation Layer: Front-end client applications providing reporting dashboards, OLAP multidimensional cubes, data visualization, and predictive data mining tools. Metadata Repository: Maintains administrative schemas, ETL business rules, transformation lineage, and indexing definitions, serving as the system directory across all warehouse components. 2. The ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) Process: Extract: Captures changed data (CDC) from heterogeneous relational databases, legacy systems, and unstructured files without interrupting live transaction processing. Transform: Performs critical data cleansing (handling null values and duplicates), standardizing disparate formats (e.g., converting dates to ISO standard, harmonizing currency codes), joining reference data, and generating artificial surrogate primary keys. Load: Executes bulk insertions of curated records into the target warehouse fact

and dimension tables during scheduled batch loading windows. 3. Role of Data Marts: A data mart is a departmental, highly focused subset of the warehouse customized for specific business units (such as Marketing, Finance, or Logistics). By structuring data into dedicated star or snowflake schemas, data marts deliver accelerated query performance, tighter security isolation, and tailored analytics without traversing the massive enterprise warehouse.

title: Why is two-phase locking (mostly strict 2PL) used in commercial DBMSs? Show with an example schedule that it can still cause deadlock, and write its other drawbacks.
chunks: Commercial database engines (such as Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server) overwhelmingly implement Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) as their primary concurrency control protocol. 1. Why Commercial DBMSs Adopt Strict 2PL: Guarantees Serializability: Like basic 2PL, it mathematically guarantees that all concurrent interleaved schedules are conflict serializable. Eliminates Cascading Aborts: By holding exclusive ($X$) locks until commit, transactions never write data that others read uncommitted; schedules are strictly cascadeless and recoverable. Simple Crash Recovery: Transaction rollback requires only undoing before-images without inspecting or aborting other transactions. 2. Deadlock Schedule Example under Strict 2PL: Strict 2PL does not prevent deadlocks. Consider two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ accessing data items $A$ and $B$: $T_1$ acquires $X(A)$ and writes to $A$. $T_2$ acquires $X(B)$ and writes to $B$. $T_1$ requests $X(B)$: since $T_2$ holds $X(B)$ until commit, $T_1$ must wait for $T_2$. $T_2$ requests $X(A)$: since $T_1$ holds $X(A)$ until commit, $T_2$ must wait for $T_1$. Both transactions hold resources while waiting for each other ($T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1$), creating a mutual deadlock that requires DBMS intervention. 3. Drawbacks of Two-Phase Locking: Deadlock Overhead: Systems must dedicate CPU cycles to maintain wait-for graphs, run cycle-detection routines, and abort/restart victims. Reduced Concurrency & Lock

Convoying: Long-running write transactions holding exclusive locks stall all subsequent readers and writers, degrading multi-user throughput. Lock Maintenance Cost: Allocating, updating, and hashing lock table entries adds memory consumption and lock manager processing latency. Phantom Anomalies: Tuple-level 2PL cannot stop phantom inserts into range queries unless expensive predicate/index-range locking is used.

title: Explain the deadlock prevention schemes Wait-Die and Wound-Wait with examples.
chunks: Deadlock prevention protocols use transaction timestamps to decide whether a requesting transaction should wait or abort when a resource conflict occurs. Monotonic timestamp $TS(T_i)$ is assigned when transaction $T_i$ begins (smaller timestamp implies older transaction). Suppose transaction $T_i$ requests a lock held by transaction $T_j$: 1. Wait-Die Scheme (Non-Preemptive): Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait . Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ dies (aborts) and restarts with its original timestamp. Rule Summary: 'Old waits, young dies.' Locks are never preemptively stolen. Example: Let $TS(T_1)=10$ (older) and $TS(T_2)=20$ (younger). If $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ waits. If $T_2$ requests a lock held by $T_1$, $T_2$ dies and restarts. 2. Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive): Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ wounds $T_j$; $T_j$ is preempted, aborted, and rolls back, releasing its lock to $T_i$. $T_j$ restarts with its original timestamp. Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait . Rule Summary: 'Old wounds, young waits.' Younger transactions are preempted by older ones. Example: With $TS(T_1)=10$ and $TS(T_2)=20$, if $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ preempts ($T_2$ is aborted). If $T_2$ requests a lock held

by $T_1$, $T_2$ waits. 3. Key Comparison: Metric Wait-Die Wound-Wait Preemption Non-preemptive Preemptive Number of Aborts High (young transactions die repeatedly) Fewer aborts; locks granted quickly to old Starvation Avoided (retains original timestamp) Avoided (retains original timestamp) Starvation Freedom Guarantee: In both schemes, when an aborted transaction restarts, it keeps its original starting timestamp. Thus, as time passes, the transaction becomes progressively older relative to new transactions, guaranteeing that it eventually becomes the oldest active transaction and runs to completion without ever dying again.

title: Construct a B+ tree in which every node can hold at most 3 keys (a maximum of 4 child pointers) by inserting the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 in the given order. Show the tree  after every node split and state two advantages of a B+ tree over a B-tree.
chunks: Node Specification: Max keys $M = 3$, maximum child pointers $P = 4$. A node splits when the number of keys reaches 4. Step-by-Step Construction: Insert 10, 20, 30: All fit in the single root leaf node: [10, 20, 30] . Insert 40 (Split 1): Node overflows to [10, 20, 30, 40] . In a B+ tree leaf split, the middle key (index $\lceil 4/2 \rceil = 2$, key 30) is copied up to the parent. Left leaf keeps [10, 20] , right leaf keeps [30, 40] with a leaf sibling pointer. New root becomes [30] . Insert 50: Placed into right leaf: [30, 40, 50] . Tree valid. Insert 60 (Split 2): Right leaf overflows to [30, 40, 50, 60] . Leaf splits: left leaf retains [30, 40] , right leaf gets [50, 60] , and key 50 is copied up to root. Root now contains keys [30, 50] . Insert 70: Placed into rightmost leaf: [50, 60, 70] . Node is full but does not exceed 3 keys. Two Distinct Advantages of a B+ Tree over a Standard B-Tree: Extremely Fast Sequential Range Queries: In a B+ tree, all leaf nodes are linked into a continuous linked list.

Range queries execute by jumping to the start key via root search and simply scanning linearly across leaf sibling pointers, completely avoiding expensive in-order tree traversals required by B-trees. Higher Fanout and Lower Tree Height: Internal nodes in a B+ tree store only search keys and child pointers without actual data records. Consequently, each fixed-size disk page fits significantly more branch pointers (higher fanout), making the tree shallower and drastically reducing the number of disk I/O operations required for lookups.

title: A static hash file uses the hash function h(k) = k mod 5. Each bucket holds at most 2 records and overflow is handled by chaining. Insert the keys 5, 12, 21, 9, 17, 14, 8, 33, 22 and 7 in the given order and show the final contents of each bucket. Also explain how extendible hashing avoids long overflow chains.
chunks: 1. Step-by-Step Hash Insertions ($h(k) = k \bmod 5$, Bucket Capacity = 2): $k = 5 \implies 5 \bmod 5 = 0$: Placed in Bucket 0 [5]. $k = 12 \implies 12 \bmod 5 = 2$: Placed in Bucket 2 [12]. $k = 21 \implies 21 \bmod 5 = 1$: Placed in Bucket 1 [21]. $k = 9 \implies 9 \bmod 5 = 4$: Placed in Bucket 4 [9]. $k = 17 \implies 17 \bmod 5 = 2$: Placed in Bucket 2 [12, 17] (Bucket 2 full). $k = 14 \implies 14 \bmod 5 = 4$: Placed in Bucket 4 [9, 14] (Bucket 4 full). $k = 8 \implies 8 \bmod 5 = 3$: Placed in Bucket 3 [8]. $k = 33 \implies 33 \bmod 5 = 3$: Placed in Bucket 3 [8, 33] (Bucket 3 full). $k = 22 \implies 22 \bmod 5 = 2$: Bucket 2 full! Overflow chain allocated $\rightarrow$ [22]. $k = 7 \implies 7 \bmod 5 = 2$: Bucket 2 overflow has space $\rightarrow$ [22, 7]. Final Contents of Buckets: Bucket No. Primary Bucket (Cap=2) Overflow Chained Bucket Bucket 0 [5] (Empty) Bucket 1 [21] (Empty) Bucket 2 [12, 17] $\rightarrow$ [22, 7] (Chained Overflow)

Bucket 3 [8, 33] (Empty) Bucket 4 [9, 14] (Empty) 2. How Extendible Hashing Avoids Long Overflow Chains: In Extendible Hashing , a dynamic directory of pointers based on prefixes/suffixes of hash bit sequences is used. When a bucket overflows, only the overflowing bucket splits into two, and its local depth increments. If the local depth exceeds the global depth, the directory size doubles, eliminating long sequential overflow chains and maintaining $O(1)$ search time.

title: A retail chain wants to analyse its sales by store, product and month. (i) Design a star schema with one fact table and suitable dimension tables. (ii) Explain the OLAP operations roll-up, drill-down and slice with an example from this schema. (iii) Analyse how the OLAP workload on this warehouse differs from the OLTP workload of the stores' billing systems.
chunks: (i) Star Schema Design: (ii) OLAP Operations: Roll-up (Aggregation): Ascends the hierarchy, generalizing data (e.g., aggregating monthly sales into quarterly or annual sales). Drill-down (De-aggregation): Descends the hierarchy into finer details (e.g., breaking annual sales down to individual store daily sales). Slice (Filtering): Selects a specific dimension slice (e.g., filtering sales strictly where region = 'West' ). (iii) OLTP vs. OLAP Comparison: Feature OLTP (Billing System) OLAP (Data Warehouse) Orientation Customer, transaction-oriented (fast inserts/updates). Management, decision-support analysis. Operations Simple read/write transactions (e.g., scan barcode, update stock). Complex aggregation queries spanning millions of historical records. Database Design Highly normalized (3NF) to eliminate anomalies. Denormalized (Star/Snowflake schema) for rapid read joins.

title: Differentiate between fragmentation and replication in a distributed database.
chunks: The core differences between fragmentation and replication in distributed databases are: Fragmentation: Divides a logical relation into non-overlapping sub-relations (horizontal rows, vertical columns, or hybrid) distributed across different sites without data duplication. Replication: Stores redundant full copies of a relation or fragment at two or more geographically distributed network sites to enhance availability and read locality.

title: State any two advantages and one drawback of data replication in a distributed database.
chunks: Data replication in distributed databases offers significant benefits and distinct trade-offs: Advantage 1 (High Availability): If a node holding data crashes, queries are transparently serviced by surviving replicas without downtime. Advantage 2 (Fast Read Performance): Read operations execute locally at the nearest replica site, eliminating wide-area network latency. Drawback (Update Overhead): Every write must be synchronized across all replicas, requiring distributed consensus protocols that increase write latency.

title: Define an index in MongoDB and state why it is used.
chunks: An index in MongoDB is a specialized auxiliary data structure (implemented as a B-tree) that stores a small portion of a collection's document fields in an easily traversable, sorted order. Why it is used: Query Acceleration: Avoids expensive full collection scans ( COLLSCAN ) by allowing the query engine to rapidly locate documents ( IXSCAN ). Efficient Sorting: Fulfills sorted queries directly from the index order without memory-intensive sort operations.

title: What is the purpose of the _id field in a MongoDB document?
chunks: The _id field serves as the mandatory primary key for every document in a MongoDB collection, uniquely identifying it within that collection. Default Generation: If omitted during insertion, MongoDB automatically populates _id with a unique 12-byte ObjectId (composed of timestamp, machine identifier, process ID, and incrementing counter). Unique Index: MongoDB automatically builds and maintains a unique index on _id , ensuring fast document lookups and preventing duplicate keys.

title: State the CAP theorem and name its three properties.
chunks: Brewer's CAP Theorem states that any distributed data store can simultaneously guarantee at most two out of three properties in the presence of network partitions. Its three core properties are: Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error. Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a non-error response for every request (without guaranteeing latest data). Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate despite arbitrary network message losses or node network isolations.

title: What is a replica set in MongoDB?
chunks: A replica set in MongoDB is a cluster of mongod processes that maintain identical data copies to provide high availability and automatic failover. Primary Node: Exactly one primary receives all write operations, recording modifications in its replication operation log ( oplog ). Secondary Nodes: Multiple secondaries continuously replicate the primary's oplog and apply operations asynchronously. If the primary fails, secondaries elect a new primary via consensus.

title: Define sharding and state why it is used in MongoDB.
chunks: Sharding is a method for distributing data horizontally across multiple machines or clusters using a designated partition field known as a shard key . Why it is used in MongoDB: Horizontal Scalability (Scale-Out): Overcomes the hardware limits (RAM, CPU, disk I/O) of a single server by adding affordable commodity servers. Throughput Distribution: Partitions massive data sets and splits high-volume read/write query loads across independent shard servers.

title: Explain the main types of NoSQL databases and give one example product for each type.
chunks: NoSQL databases diverge from relational models by adopting non-tabular, flexible storage architectures: Key-Value Store: Stores data as associative arrays of unique keys paired with arbitrary binary values. Highly optimized for simple $O(1)$ lookups and session caches. Example: Redis , Amazon DynamoDB. Document-Oriented Database: Stores semi-structured data as self-describing BSON/JSON documents with nested objects and arrays, eliminating fixed relational schemas. Example: MongoDB , Couchbase. Column-Family (Wide-Column) Store: Organizes data into columns grouped into column families rather than rows, enabling high compression and massive analytical read throughput. Example: Apache Cassandra , Apache HBase. Graph Database: Represents data as nodes (entities) and edges (explicit relationships) with key-value properties, designed for complex network traversals without recursive relational joins. Example: Neo4j , Amazon Neptune.

title: Describe how data is organised in MongoDB into databases, collections and documents, with an example.
chunks: MongoDB organizes data hierarchically into three structural levels: Database: The outermost container that manages a physical set of files on disk. A single MongoDB instance can host multiple independent databases (e.g., universityDB ). Collection: A group of related documents housed inside a database, analogous to a relational table. However, collections are schema-free : documents in a collection do not need identical fields. Document: The fundamental atomic unit of data, serialized and stored in Binary JSON (BSON). Each document contains field-value pairs supporting nested objects, arrays, and an immutable _id primary key. Hierarchical Example: // Inside database: universityDB, collection: students { "_id": ObjectId("64a1b2c3d4e5f67890123456"), "rollNo": 101, "name": "Alice", "dept": "CSE", "address": { "city": "Bengaluru", "pincode": 560001 }, "courses": ["DBMS", "OS", "Networks"] }

title: Define a distributed database. Give two advantages and two challenges of such systems.
chunks: A distributed database is a collection of multiple logically interrelated databases distributed across different physical locations connected via a computer network, managed by a centralized Distributed DBMS (DDBMS). Two Advantages: Local Autonomy & Improved Performance: Sites maintain control over local data, allowing frequently accessed local queries to execute with zero network delay. High Availability and Reliability: Data replication ensures that if one server or geographical site suffers a failure, surviving nodes continue processing requests without system outages. Two Challenges: Complexity of Distributed Transactions: Maintaining ACID properties requires complex multi-phase commit protocols (e.g., 2PC) that increase latency and deadlock vulnerabilities. Network Overhead and Security: Latency across wide-area communication links impacts throughput, while distributed network endpoints expand the surface area for security threats.

title: Define a cloud database. Discuss its advantages and limitations compared with an on -premise database.
chunks: A cloud database is a database service deployed, configured, and accessed through a cloud platform (e.g., AWS RDS, Google Cloud Spanner, MongoDB Atlas), typically delivered as Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS). Advantages over On-Premise Databases: Elastic Scalability: Compute and storage resources can be scaled up or out dynamically with a single click or API call to match workload spikes. Automated Administration: Routine maintenance (patching, automated backups, hardware provisioning, failover) is managed transparently by the cloud vendor. Cost Efficiency: Eliminates upfront capital expenditure for enterprise server hardware, utilizing an operational pay-as-you-go model. Limitations: Vendor Lock-in: Migrating proprietary configurations and stored procedures between different cloud providers is technically challenging and expensive. Data Sovereignty & Network Dependency: Sensitive corporate data must comply with geographic compliance regulations (GDPR/HIPAA), and database availability is bound to external internet connection stability.

title: A MongoDB collection employees contains documents of the form {empid, nam e, dept, salary}. Write queries to (i) find the employees working in 'IT' or 'HR' using the $in operator and (ii) find the employees earning more than 50000, sorted by salary in descending order.
chunks: Given the employees collection schema {empid, name, dept, salary} , the required MongoDB queries are: (i) Employees working in 'IT' or 'HR' using the $in operator: db.employees.find({ dept: { $in: ["IT", "HR"] } }); Explanation: The $in comparison operator performs an equality match against an array of specified literal values, selecting any document where dept is either 'IT' or 'HR'. (ii) Employees earning more than 50,000, sorted by salary descending: db.employees.find({ salary: { $gt: 50000 } }).sort({ salary: -1 }); Explanation: The $gt operator filters records having salary strictly greater than 50,000. Chaining .sort({ salary: -1 }) orders output in descending order (-1 denotes descending, 1 denotes ascending).

title: A MongoDB collection students contains documents of the form {rollNo, name, dept, age, marks}. Write queries to (i) find the students aged between 18 and 22 (inclusive) using $gte and $lte, (ii) display only the name and marks of students who scored above 75, and (iii) count the students of the 'CSE' department.
chunks: Given collection students with schema {rollNo, name, dept, age, marks} : (i) Students aged between 18 and 22 inclusive: db.students.find({ age: { $gte: 18, $lte: 22 } }); Explanation: Combines $gte (greater than or equal) and $lte (less than or equal) inside the age field object. (ii) Display only name and marks of students scoring above 75: db.students.find( { marks: { $gt: 75 } }, { name: 1, marks: 1, _id: 0 } ); Explanation: The second argument defines a projection document: 1 includes fields, while _id: 0 explicitly suppresses the default primary key. (iii) Count students in the 'CSE' department: db.students.countDocuments({ dept: "CSE" }); Explanation: countDocuments() returns the accurate scalar integer count of matching documents.

title: Choose the most suitable type of NoSQL database (key-value, document, column-family or graph) for each case and justify your choice: (i) caching of user login sessions, (ii) a product catalogue with varying attributes, and (iii) friend recommendations on a social network.
chunks: Selection and justification of NoSQL database types for each use case: (i) Caching of User Login Sessions: Key-Value Database (e.g., Redis). Justification: A session token acts as a unique primary key pointing to user state. In-memory key-value stores deliver sub-millisecond $O(1)$ read/write latency with native TTL key expiration for automatic session timeouts. (ii) Product Catalogue with Varying Attributes: Document Database (e.g., MongoDB). Justification: Products have radically diverse attributes (laptops have CPU/RAM, shoes have size/color). A document model supports polymorphic JSON schemas where documents define custom attributes without sparse, null-filled relational columns. (iii) Friend Recommendations on a Social Network: Graph Database (e.g., Neo4j). Justification: Social platforms rely on interconnected networks. Graph databases represent users as nodes and friendships as direct edges, executing multi-hop traversals in milliseconds without recursive SQL joins.

title: Explain the BASE properties of NoSQL databases and contrast them briefly with ACID.
chunks: The BASE model governs distributed NoSQL systems, prioritizing horizontal availability over strict relational consistency: Basically Available: The database system remains operational and accessible to clients at all times, even in the event of partial node or network partition failures. Soft State: System state may fluctuate or drift over time even without client interaction, due to asynchronous replica propagation models. Eventual Consistency: The system does not guarantee immediate consistency on every read, but guarantees that all replicas will eventually converge to identical states if no further updates occur. Contrast with ACID: Pessimistic vs. Optimistic: ACID enforces strict, immediate consistency and serializable isolation via pessimistic locking, causing operations to stall or fail during partitions. Availability Priority: BASE embraces optimistic, relaxed consistency to guarantee uninterrupted availability ($A$) and partition tolerance ($P$) across large distributed clusters.

title: Differentiate between structured, semi-structured and unstructured data with one example of each.
chunks: Data in modern information architectures is categorized into three structural paradigms: Structured Data: Conforms to a strict, predefined tabular schema with fixed columns, specific data types, and explicit relational keys. Easily queried and manipulated using standard SQL. Example: An RDBMS relational table (e.g., Employee(EmpID, Name, Salary, HireDate) ) or CSV spreadsheets. Semi-Structured Data: Does not conform to a rigid relational schema, but contains internal organizational markers, tags, or hierarchies that separate individual data elements. Example: JSON documents, XML files, or BSON records (e.g., {"name": "Alice", "skills": ["DBMS", "Java"]} ). Unstructured Data: Data that has no predefined conceptual schema, model, or internal organizational structure. Requires specialized AI/ML algorithms or full-text parsing to extract meaning. Example: Video files, MP3 audio recordings, satellite imagery, and free-form scanned medical PDF reports.

title: A MongoDB collection orders contains documents of the form {orderId, custId, status, amount}. Write an aggregation pipeline to find the total amount of 'Delivered' orders for each customer, sorted in descending order of the total. Explain the role of each stage used.
chunks: The MongoDB aggregation pipeline processes documents through a multi-stage data transformation sequence: db.orders.aggregate([ { $match: { status: "Delivered" } }, { $group: { _id: "$custId", totalAmount: { $sum: "$amount" } } }, { $sort: { totalAmount: -1 } } ]); Explanation of Pipeline Stages: Stage 1 ( $match ): Acts as an initial filter stage (analogous to SQL WHERE ). Passes only documents where status === "Delivered" to downstream stages, dramatically minimizing subsequent memory overhead. Stage 2 ( $group ): Groups the filtered stream by the customer identifier ( _id: "$custId" ) (analogous to SQL GROUP BY ). It computes the aggregated metric totalAmount using the accumulator operator $sum: "$amount" . Stage 3 ( $sort ): Reorders the grouped output documents in descending order of totalAmount (-1 indicates descending sort order, analogous to SQL ORDER BY totalAmount DESC ).

title: Differentiate between insertOne and insertMany, updateOne and updateMany, and deleteOne and deleteMany in MongoDB, giving a one-line command for each.
chunks: MongoDB distinguishes between single-document and multi-document CRUD methods: insertOne vs. insertMany: insertOne inserts a single document into the collection. db.users.insertOne({ name: "Alice", age: 21 }); insertMany inserts an array of multiple documents in a single atomic batch call. db.users.insertMany([{ name: "Bob" }, { name: "Carol" }]); updateOne vs. updateMany: updateOne updates only the first matching document encountered in the collection. db.users.updateOne({ name: "Alice" }, { $set: { age: 22 } }); updateMany updates all documents in the collection that satisfy the query filter. db.users.updateMany({ dept: "HR" }, { $inc: { salary: 2000 } }); deleteOne vs. deleteMany: deleteOne removes at most one document matching the specified criteria. db.users.deleteOne({ name: "Bob" }); deleteMany deletes every document satisfying the filter condition. db.users.deleteMany({ status: "inactive" });

title: Explain how an index improves query performance in MongoDB. Write commands to (i) create an ascending index on the field name of the collection students, (ii) create a compound index on dept (ascending) and cgpa (descending), and (iii) create a unique index on rollno.
chunks: An index creates an ordered auxiliary B-tree structure mapping indexed field values to their physical document locations (RecordID) on disk. Without an index, MongoDB executes a full collection scan ( COLLSCAN ), examining every document in memory. With an index, it performs an index scan ( IXSCAN ), jumping directly to matching keys in $O(\log N)$ time. Index Creation Commands: (i) Ascending index on field name : db.students.createIndex({ name: 1 }); Explanation: 1 specifies an ascending index order. (ii) Compound index on dept (ascending) and cgpa (descending): db.students.createIndex({ dept: 1, cgpa: -1 }); Explanation: Indexes multiple fields together, accelerating queries that filter on dept and sort by cgpa . (iii) Unique index on field rollno : db.students.createIndex({ rollno: 1 }, { unique: true }); Explanation: The { unique: true } constraint causes MongoDB to reject any insert or update with duplicate rollno values.

title: In a MongoDB collection students whose documents look like {rollno, n ame, dept, cgpa, skills: [...]}, write commands to (i) list the name and cgpa of 'CSE' students whose cgpa is above 8, (ii) add 0.2 to the cgpa of the student with rollno 12, and (iii) remove every student whose cgpa is below 5.
chunks: Given the MongoDB collection students with schema {rollno, name, dept, cgpa, skills: [...]} , the required CRUD operations and execution semantics are structured as follows: (i) List the name and cgpa of 'CSE' students whose cgpa is above 8: db.students.find( { dept: "CSE", cgpa: { $gt: 8 } }, { name: 1, cgpa: 1, _id: 0 } ); Explanation: The query filter applies an implicit logical AND across both conditions: dept: "CSE" and the comparison operator cgpa: { $gt: 8 } . The second argument defines the projection specification, where name: 1 and cgpa: 1 include those fields in the output, while _id: 0 explicitly suppresses the default primary key field. (ii) Add 0.2 to the cgpa of the student with rollno 12: db.students.updateOne( { rollno: 12 }, { $inc: { cgpa: 0.2 } } ); Explanation: updateOne() targets the first document matching { rollno: 12 } . The $inc field update operator atomically increments the numeric value of cgpa by 0.2. In MongoDB, single-document updates are strictly atomic, eliminating race conditions without requiring an explicit transaction block. (iii) Remove every student whose cgpa is below 5: db.students.deleteMany({ cgpa: { $lt: 5 } }); Explanation: deleteMany() removes all documents in

the collection that satisfy the filter condition { cgpa: { $lt: 5 } } , using the less-than operator $lt . It returns an acknowledged write result object displaying the exact count of deleted documents. Indexing Optimization Note: To ensure high performance at scale, creating a compound index with db.students.createIndex({ dept: 1, cgpa: -1 }) enables the query engine to execute query (i) as an index scan ( IXSCAN ) instead of scanning every document in memory ( COLLSCAN ).

title: A MongoDB collection employees stores documents of the form {empid, name, dept, salary}. Write queries to (i) fetch the employees of the 'HR' department, (ii) fetch the employees earning more than 40000 using the $gt operator, and (iii) show only the name and salary of all em ployees in ascending order of salary.
chunks: Given the collection employees storing documents of the structure {empid, name, dept, salary} , the required query operations and execution mechanics are formulated as follows: (i) Fetch the employees of the 'HR' department: db.employees.find({ dept: "HR" }); Explanation: Performs an exact equality match against the dept field, retrieving all documents where the department string equals 'HR'. If no projection document is supplied as the second parameter, MongoDB returns all document fields including _id , empid , name , and salary . (ii) Fetch the employees earning more than 40,000 using the $gt operator: db.employees.find({ salary: { $gt: 40000 } }); Explanation: Utilizes the comparison operator $gt (greater than) within the criteria to filter and return documents where the numeric salary attribute strictly exceeds 40,000. (iii) Show only the name and salary of all employees in ascending order of salary: db.employees.find( {}, { name: 1, salary: 1, _id: 0 } ).sort({ salary: 1 }); Explanation: An empty query document {} matches all records in the collection. The projection document { name: 1, salary: 1, _id: 0 } restricts output exclusively to name and salary , while suppressing the default _id field. Chaining the cursor modifier .sort({ salary: 1 }) sorts the

output in ascending order of salary (where 1 denotes ascending and -1 denotes descending). Memory & Index Considerations: In MongoDB, in-memory sort operations are capped at 32 MB of RAM. Creating an index on { salary: 1 } allows MongoDB to retrieve sorted documents directly from the index tree without loading the entire collection into memory or exceeding sort RAM limits.

title: A start-up e-commerce company must handle (i) customer orders and payments, (ii) a product catalogue in which products have widely differing attributes, and (iii) millions of daily click -stream events and product recommendations. For each requirement, analyse whether an RDBMS or a NoSQL store such as MongoDB is more suitable, considering schema flexibility, consistency, scalability and joins.
chunks: Part 1: E-Commerce Architectural Analysis: (i) Customer Orders & Payments: RDBMS (e.g., PostgreSQL). Justification: Financial ledgers require strict ACID guarantees, multi-table foreign key constraints, and serializable isolation to prevent double payments or lost inventory. Financial records require immediate consistency and complex relational joins across tables (Customers, Orders, Payments, Invoices) that RDBMS handles natively. (ii) Product Catalogue with Diverse Attributes: NoSQL Document Store (MongoDB). Justification: Products possess widely variable attributes (e.g., laptops have RAM/storage, shirts have size/fabric). Relational databases require hundreds of sparse, null-filled columns or complex Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) tables that ruin join performance. MongoDB's dynamic BSON schema allows polymorphic documents to coexist naturally in a single collection. (iii) Clickstream Events & Recommendations: Distributed NoSQL / Column Store (e.g., Cassandra / Redis). Justification: High-velocity clickstream ingest produces massive write volumes (millions of clicks/sec) that exceed RDBMS vertical scale limits. Distributed NoSQL stores provide horizontal sharding, high write throughput, and linear scalability under relaxed BASE consistency. Requirement Chosen Engine Schema Consistency Scalability Orders & Payments RDBMS Rigid Tabular Immediate (ACID) Vertical (Scale-up) Product Catalog MongoDB Flexible BSON Document Atomic Horizontal (Sharding) Clickstreams NoSQL (Cassandra/Redis) Key-Value/Column Eventual (BASE) Linear Scale-out Part 2: MongoDB Queries on Collection products : (i) Products in 'Electronics' or

'Furniture' using $or : db.products.find({ $or: [ { category: "Electronics" }, { category: "Furniture" } ] }); (ii) Products priced between 1,000 and 5,000 inclusive: db.products.find({ price: { $gte: 1000, $lte: 5000 } }); (iii) Display only productName of the five costliest products: db.products.find( {}, { productName: 1, _id: 0 } ).sort({ price: -1 }).limit(5);

title: In a MongoDB collection products with documents of the form {productId, productName, category, price}, write queries to (i) find the products in the 'Electronics' or 'Furniture' category using the $or operator, (ii) find the products priced between 1000 and 5000 using $gte and $lte, and (iii) display only the productName of the five costliest products.
