title: A social media platform produces about 5 TB of posts, images, videos and 'like' events every day. Analyse this scenario in terms of volume, velocity, variety and veracity, explain why a traditional RDBMS struggles with it, and recommend suitable Big Data/NoSQL databases, giving one reason for each.
chunks: 1. Analysis of the Scenario via Big Data 4Vs: Volume: Generating 5 TB of raw data daily equates to ~150 TB/month and petabytes over years, far exceeding single-node server storage capacities. Velocity: Millions of concurrent user actions (likes, comments, video streams) arrive every second, demanding sub-millisecond ingest write speeds and real-time feed updates. Variety: Data encompasses structured user account profiles, semi-structured JSON post threads, and massive unstructured binary media (MP4 videos, JPEG images). Veracity: High proportion of noisy, duplicated, or unverified interactions (spam bots, rapid double-clicks, corrupted network packets) that require filtering. 2. Why a Traditional RDBMS Struggles: Vertical Scaling Bottlenecks: Traditional RDBMSs scale vertically (bigger CPU/RAM on one machine). A single server cannot process 5 TB daily write IOPS. Rigid Relational Schemas: RDBMS cannot dynamically ingest polymorphic post formats or evolving video metadata without costly schema migrations and table locks. Lock Contention & Joins: Strict ACID row-level locking causes severe lock contention on hot records (celebrity posts), and recursive multi-table SQL joins across petabytes of rows crush query latency. 3. Recommended Big Data / NoSQL Architecture: In-Memory Key-Value Store (Redis): For real-time 'like' counters, trending hashtags, and user session tokens with sub-millisecond in-memory caching and atomic increments. Wide-Column Distributed

Store (Apache Cassandra): For activity timeline feeds and interaction audit logs; provides masterless distributed writes across clusters with linear horizontal scaling and zero single point of failure. Distributed Object Store (Amazon S3 / Ceph) + CDN: For massive unstructured video and image media files, while keeping lightweight metadata and CDN URLs in MongoDB. Architectural Paradigm: Modern social architectures utilize a Lambda Architecture , separating high-velocity ingestion (speed layer via Kafka/Cassandra) from long-term analytical batch processing (Hadoop/Spark) under eventual consistency.

title: A university stores student attendance, examination results, course registrations and feedback in a MongoDB collection students with documents of the form {rollno, name, attendance, marks, feedback: [...]}. Explain how MongoDB's flexible schema and document model suit such records better than fixed relational tables, and write queries to (i) find the students with attendance below 75, (ii) find the students with marks above 80, and (iii) find the students who satisfy both conditions.
chunks: 1. Architectural Suitability of MongoDB's Document Model: Elimination of Relational Joins: In an RDBMS, this scenario requires four normalized tables ( Students , Attendance , ExamMarks , Feedback ) connected via foreign keys, requiring expensive multi-table SQL joins. MongoDB nests attendance, marks, and an array of feedback subdocuments into a single document, retrieving complete student records in a single disk read. Polymorphic Schema Flexibility: Different academic departments have varying feedback templates, optional elective fields, and grading criteria. MongoDB's dynamic schema allows documents to store custom department fields without requiring schema alterations or creating sparse tables with null columns. Natural 1-to-Many Representation: The feedback: [...] array natively encapsulates embedded subdocuments (with instructor name, rating, comments), preserving document locality on disk. Document Schema Validation: MongoDB supports JSON Schema validation to enforce data integrity (e.g., verifying cgpa >= 0 and attendance <= 100 ) while retaining complete field flexibility. 2. MongoDB Queries: (i) Students with attendance below 75: db.students.find({ attendance: { $lt: 75 } }); Explanation: The $lt operator matches all student records whose attendance percentage is strictly under 75. (ii) Students with marks above 80: db.students.find({ marks: { $gt: 80 } }); Explanation: The $gt operator filters records where academic marks exceed

80. (iii) Students who satisfy both conditions (attendance < 75 AND marks > 80): db.students.find({ attendance: { $lt: 75 }, marks: { $gt: 80 } }); Explanation: Specifying comma-separated field criteria in a single query document enforces an implicit boolean AND condition, returning students with poor attendance who nevertheless achieved high marks.

title: A healthcare organisation collects patient records, medical reports, diagnostic images and real -time data from wearable devices. Analyse the challenges that such diverse, continuously generated data creates for a traditional relational database. Explain how MongoDB's flexible schema, sharding and replication help meet these challenges, and describe how the large diagnostic images can be stored (for example with GridFS or an object store with metadata kept in MongoDB), justifying your choice.
chunks: 1. Challenges for a Traditional Relational Database: Schema Rigidity: Medical reports and clinical lab tests vary wildly across specializations (cardiology, oncology). Enforcing rigid relational tables causes extensive schema bloat, dozens of null columns, and costly ALTER TABLE lockups. High-Velocity Time-Series Streaming: Continuous wearable telemetry (heart rate, SpO2) produces millions of timestamped write events per minute, overwhelming RDBMS single-server disk I/O and transaction logging. Large Binary Data Overhead: High-resolution medical imaging (MRI, CT scans in DICOM format, often 50 MB to 1 GB) stored as database BLOBs exhausts memory buffers, degrades backup speeds, and hampers query performance. 2. How MongoDB Addresses These Challenges: Flexible Schema: JSON/BSON document model naturally accommodates heterogeneous patient profiles, varying lab diagnostics, and dynamic doctor prescriptions. Sharding: Horizontally distributes streaming IoT wearable vitals across multiple shard nodes using a compound shard key (e.g., { patientId: 1, timestamp: 1 } ), balancing write throughput. Replication: Multi-node replica sets ensure 99.999% clinical availability, disaster recovery, and zero data loss during hardware failures. 3. Storing Diagnostic Images (Architecture & Justification): GridFS: MongoDB's specification for storing files exceeding the 16 MB document limit by automatically splitting binaries into 255 KB chunks across fs.files and fs.chunks collections. Recommended Approach (Hybrid Object Store

+ MongoDB): Store high-resolution binary DICOM image files in a dedicated cloud object store (e.g., Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage) and store rich clinical metadata (Patient ID, scan date, modality, S3 presigned URL, AI diagnosis tags) inside MongoDB. Justification: Cloud object stores offer lower per-gigabyte storage costs, native CDN integration for hospital workstations, and keep MongoDB working-set RAM lean and dedicated to high-speed clinical metadata indexing.

title: Analyse the suitability of MongoDB for (i) storing IoT sensor readings and (ii) a content management system of a news website. For each, justify your decision by discussing schema  flexibility, scalability and consistency/transaction needs, and mention one more real-world application where MongoDB fits well.
chunks: MongoDB's document-oriented architecture provides compelling advantages across specific industry workloads: (i) IoT Sensor Readings: Schema Flexibility: Diverse sensors (temperature, vibration, pressure, GPS) produce disparate payload structures. MongoDB easily ingests varying JSON metrics without requiring rigid column definitions. Scalability: High-frequency telemetry streams are partitioned across clusters via horizontal sharding . Native time-series collections (specifying timeField and metaField ) optimize storage footprint through automated bucket compression and columnar disk layouts. Consistency & Transactions: IoT streams tolerate eventual consistency. Configurable write concerns (e.g., { w: 1 } ) maximize write throughput over strict multi-document serializability. Verdict: Highly Suitable for massive, append-only sensor telemetry. (ii) Content Management System (CMS) of a News Website: Schema Flexibility: News stories feature rich, evolving structures: varied multimedia embeds, editorial revision histories, author arrays, and tagging hierarchies. The document model represents an entire article and its comments natively in a single BSON document. Scalability: Breaking news generates massive read spikes. MongoDB handles high read volume via replica sets , directing queries to secondary nodes using nearest or secondaryPreferred read preferences. Consistency & Transactions: Publishing an article is an atomic, single-document write; MongoDB provides native single-document ACID transactions, satisfying editorial publishing requirements. Verdict: Extremely Well-Suited for high-read, semi-structured editorial content.

Additional Real-World Application: E-Commerce Product Catalog. E-commerce catalogs feature millions of products with wildly heterogeneous attributes (e.g., electronics, apparel, groceries). MongoDB stores polymorphic products within a single collection, supports fast multi-attribute compound indexing, and enables rapid catalog search without expensive SQL joins. Additionally, multikey indexes on embedded arrays enable instant filtering on multi-valued product tags (such as available sizes, colors, and technical specifications) without maintaining separate relational junction tables.

title: Explain replication in MongoDB with reference to the primary and secondary members of a replica set, the election of a new primary when the current primary fails, and write concern. State the benefits of replication.
chunks: Replication in MongoDB provides redundancy, high availability, and automated failover across distributed nodes. 1. Replica Set Architecture: Primary Member: Exactly one primary accepts all write operations, recording changes in a capped collection called the oplog (operations log) . Secondary Members: Secondaries continuously read the primary's oplog and apply operations asynchronously to replicate data state. They can serve read queries if configured. Arbiter (Optional): A lightweight voting-only member that holds no data, used solely to break election ties in clusters with even node counts. 2. Election of a New Primary: Members send heartbeat pings every 2 seconds. If secondaries receive no response from the primary within 10 seconds, an election is triggered. Secondaries nominate eligible members based on member priority and oplog recency; the node holding the most up-to-date oplog that wins a strict majority of votes becomes the new Primary. 3. Write Concern: Write concern specifies the level of acknowledgement requested from MongoDB for write operations: { w: 1 } : Acknowledged by Primary only (fast, but data could be lost if primary fails before replication). { w: "majority" } : Acknowledged only after the write is committed to a majority of replica set nodes, preventing rollback during failover. {

j: true } : Ensures the operation is written to on-disk journal before returning acknowledgement. 4. Benefits of Replication: Guarantees continuous 24/7 high availability, eliminates single points of failure, allows zero-downtime rolling maintenance/upgrades, and offloads heavy analytical read traffic from the primary node. Strong write concerns (such as w: 'majority' ) protect mission-critical applications against data rollbacks if a primary node suddenly experiences ungraceful hardware failure before replication completes.

title: A MongoDB collection students contains documents of the form {rollno, name, dept, cgpa, skills: [...]}. Write aggregation pipelines to (i) display the number of students in each department, (ii) display the departments whose average cgpa is greater than 7.5 along with that average, and (iii) display the number of students having each skill using $unwind.
chunks: The MongoDB Aggregation Framework transforms document streams through multi-stage pipelines to perform complex analytical data transformations: (i) Display the number of students in each department: db.students.aggregate([ { $group: { _id: "$dept", studentCount: { $sum: 1 } } } ]); Explanation: The $group stage groups documents by the dept field ( _id: "$dept" ). The accumulator expression { $sum: 1 } increments a counter by 1 for each document in the group, outputting the department name and total headcount. (ii) Display departments whose average cgpa is greater than 7.5 along with the average: db.students.aggregate([ { $group: { _id: "$dept", avgCgpa: { $avg: "$cgpa" } } }, { $match: { avgCgpa: { $gt: 7.5 } } } ]); Explanation: Stage 1 computes the average CGPA per department using { $avg: "$cgpa" } . Stage 2 applies a $match filter on the aggregated metric, acting like SQL HAVING avgCgpa > 7.5 to retain only qualifying departments. (iii) Display the number of students having each skill using $unwind : db.students.aggregate([ { $unwind: "$skills" }, { $group: { _id: "$skills", count: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $sort: { count: -1 } } ]); Explanation: $unwind deconstructs the skills array field, generating a separate

clone document for each array element. The subsequent $group stage groups by individual skill name and counts occurrences with { $sum: 1 } . Finally, $sort arranges skills in descending order of student popularity. Pipeline Performance Note: Each aggregation stage has a 100 MB RAM limit. For large collections, enabling { allowDiskUse: true } ensures that memory-intensive grouping and sorting stages can spill intermediate data to disk temporary files.

title: Analyse the trade-offs of the CAP theorem for a distributed database during a network partition. Using this analysis, justify whether a CP or an AP design is more suitable for (i) an online banking ledger and (ii) a social-media news feed, and explain how sharding and replication help a NoSQL system to scale.
chunks: 1. CAP Theorem Trade-Off Analysis during Network Partition: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency ($C$), Availability ($A$), and Partition Tolerance ($P$). Because physical network partitions ($P$) (cable cuts, packet loss, hardware switch failures) are unavoidable in distributed architectures, systems must choose between Consistency or Availability when a partition occurs: CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): Rejects the read/write request on the isolated partition to prevent stale or conflicting data, returning an error or timeout. Sacrifices Availability to preserve absolute mathematical correctness. AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): Returns the locally available value (even if stale) and accepts writes locally. Sacrifices immediate Consistency to guarantee 100% Availability. 2. Application Justifications: (i) Online Banking Ledger: CP Design (e.g., Google Spanner, MongoDB with majority write concern). Justification: Financial ledgers require zero tolerance for dirty reads, phantom withdrawals, or double-spending. If a network partition prevents verifying account balances across branches, the system must abort the transaction rather than serve incorrect monetary balances. (ii) Social-Media News Feed: AP Design (e.g., Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB). Justification: User experience demands seamless, uninterrupted availability. If a user sees a friend's post or like count 5 seconds late due to a network partition, the business

impact is negligible compared to showing a broken error screen. 3. How Sharding and Replication Enable NoSQL Scaling: Sharding (Horizontal Scale-Out): Splits massive collections into disjoint ranges based on a shard key, distributing storage and write throughput across dozens of commodity servers. Replication (High Availability & Read Scaling): Maintains identical copies across nodes, eliminating single points of failure and distributing read query loads geographically.

Unit I: Intro & ER DBMS

Definition A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. It allows users to create, read, update, and delete data in a database. Advantages over File-Processing Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere. Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files. Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0). Security Problems: Offers fine-grained access control and user authorization. Concurrent Access: Manages simultaneous access securely, preventing anomalies. Data redundancy and data inconsistency

Definitions Data Redundancy: The unnecessary duplication of data in a database. (e.g., storing a student's address in both the Library and Department files). Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department). DBMS Solution A DBMS minimizes redundancy by storing a single, centralized copy of the data (Data Normalization). Because there is only one authoritative copy, inconsistency is inherently prevented. Give the difference between a database system and a file-based system

Differences Structure: DB systems store data in structured formats (tables/graphs); File systems store data in plain text/binary files. Data Independence: DB systems separate applications from data structure; File systems tightly couple applications to file formats. Querying: DB systems provide robust query languages (SQL); File systems require custom application code to extract data. Draw and explain the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS

The Three Levels External Level (View Level): The highest level, describing only the part of the database relevant to a specific user group (hiding the rest). Conceptual Level (Logical Level): Describes what data is stored in the entire database and the relationships among those data. Used by DBAs. Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations). Exam Tip: The primary objective of this architecture is to achieve Data Independence . Data abstraction

Definition Data abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal data structures and storage details from the user, presenting only a simplified, usable view of the data. Three Levels Physical Level: Hides the complexity of block structures, indexing, and bytes on disk. Logical Level: Hides physical storage but reveals entities, data types, and relationships. Developers interact here. View Level: Hides the entire logical schema except for specific fields the end-user is authorized to see (e.g., a teller seeing only names and balances). Terms schema and instance

Definition Schema: The overall logical design/blueprint of the database. It changes rarely. Instance: The snapshot of data residing in the database at a specific moment in time. It changes frequently. Importance This distinction is crucial for maintaining data independence—altering the schema (like adding a column) should not arbitrarily destroy the existing instances. Data independence

Definition Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition in one level without affecting a schema definition in the next higher level. Types Physical Data Independence: Ability to modify the internal/physical schema without altering the conceptual schema. Example: Changing a file from sequential to a B+ tree index to improve performance; application code doesn't change. Logical Data Independence: Ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering the external schema (user views). Example: Splitting an Employee table into two normalized tables; the original view can be maintained using a SQL JOIN, shielding the frontend application. Who are the different types of database users

Types of Users Parametric (Naive) Users: End-users who interact via standard GUI applications without knowing SQL (e.g., Bank Tellers). Application Programmers: Software engineers who write the backend logic connecting to the DB. Sophisticated Users: Analysts who interact directly with the DB using SQL queries to generate reports. Database Administrators (DBA): IT professionals who manage security, schemas, and performance tuning. List the responsibilities of a Database Administrator (DBA)

Responsibilities Schema definition and modification. Defining storage structures and access methods (indexing). Granting user authority and managing access security. Routine maintenance, database backups, and performance monitoring. Hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented data models

Comparison Hierarchical: Data organized in a tree structure (1:N relationships). Fast but inflexible; requires navigating rigid pointers. Network: Data organized in a graph (M:N relationships allowed). Highly complex and difficult to maintain. Relational: Data organized in 2D tables (relations). Uses declarative SQL. Extremely flexible and mathematically sound. Object-Oriented: Data stored as objects with methods, matching OOP languages. Best for complex data (e.g., CAD/CAM). Most Widely Used The Relational Model is most widely used today due to its simplicity, robust theoretical foundation (normalization), and standard interface (SQL) which provides unparalleled data independence. Advantages of the relational model over the other data models

Advantages Simplicity: Uses a simple tabular structure (rows and columns) that is easy to understand compared to complex graph/tree pointers. Flexibility: Supports ad-hoc querying using standard SQL. Data Independence: Strong separation between logical representation and physical storage. Terms super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key

Explanation Super Key: Any combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row. (e.g., StudentID + Name ) Candidate Key: A minimal super key; it uniquely identifies a row with no unnecessary columns. (e.g., StudentID or Email ) Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen to identify rows. Cannot be NULL. (e.g., StudentID ) Foreign Key: A column that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. (e.g., Dept_ID in a Student table referencing the Department table) Integrity constraints in a relational model

Definition Integrity constraints are rules applied to a database to ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and valid. The Four Constraints Domain Constraint: Restricts the values a column can hold to a valid set (e.g., Age must be a positive integer). Key Constraint: Ensures that candidate/primary keys are completely unique for every row. Entity Integrity: States that no part of a Primary Key can be NULL, because a NULL value cannot uniquely identify a row. Referential Integrity: States that if a foreign key exists in a relation, its value must either match a primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. (e.g., You cannot enroll a student in a non-existent Course_ID). E-R model

Definition The Entity-Relationship (E-R) model is a high-level conceptual data model that visually represents entities (objects) and the relationships between them. Notations Rectangle: Entity sets Ellipse: Attributes Diamond: Relationship sets Lines: Link attributes to entities and entities to relationships Entity, entity set, attribute and relationship, and illustrate each

Definitions Entity: A real-world object with independent existence (e.g., a specific student). Entity Set: A collection of similar entities (e.g., all Students). Attribute: A property describing an entity (e.g., Name, Age). Relationship: An association among two or more entities (e.g., Student Enroll Course). Different types of attributes, simple, composite, derived, multivalued and key attribute,

Attribute Types Simple: Indivisible atomic values (e.g., Gender ). Composite: Can be broken down into sub-parts (e.g., Name into First Name, Last Name). Derived: Calculated from other attributes; not physically stored (e.g., Age derived from DOB). Multivalued: Can hold multiple values for a single entity (e.g., Phone_Numbers ). Key: Uniquely identifies the entity (e.g., Roll_No ). Different types of relationships that can exist between two entities

Cardinality Ratios One-to-One (1:1): One entity in A is associated with at most one in B. (e.g., Department 1:1 Manager). One-to-Many (1:N): One entity in A is associated with many in B. (e.g., Department 1:N Employees). Many-to-Many (M:N): Many entities in A associated with many in B. (e.g., Student M:N Course). Weak entity set

Definition A weak entity set lacks sufficient attributes to form a primary key. It depends on a strong entity (identifying owner) and uses the owner's key plus its own partial key to identify rows. Example A Dependent (spouse/child) of an Employee. The dependent is identified by combining their Name (partial key) with the owner's Employee ID. Unary, binary and ternary relationships

Degrees of Relationships Unary (Degree 1): Relationship between instances of a single entity set (e.g., Employee Manages Employee). Binary (Degree 2): Relationship between two entity sets (e.g., Student Takes Course). Ternary (Degree 3): Relationship connecting three entity sets simultaneously (e.g., Supplier Supplies Part To Project). Exam Tip: A ternary relationship is not just three binary relationships; it represents a single fact involving all three entities together. Total participation and partial participation constraints in an E-R diagram

Differentiation Total Participation (Mandatory): Every entity MUST participate in at least one relationship. Indicated by a double line. (e.g., Every Employee must belong to a Department). Partial Participation (Optional): Only some entities may participate. Indicated by a single line. (e.g., Only some Employees are Managers of a Department). Generalization and specialization in the Extended E-R model

Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from a single entity type (the superclass). It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others. Example: An Employee superclass can be specialized into Engineer , Manager , and Technician subclasses based on job role. Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse process of specialization. Multiple entity types with common attributes are synthesized into a single, generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck entities share attributes like Vehicle_ID and Price, so they can be generalized into a Vehicle superclass. Overlapping and disjoint specialization

Disjoint Specialization An entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by a 'd' in the circle. Example: An Employee can be either an Hourly_Employee or a Salaried_Employee , but never both at the same time. Overlapping Specialization An entity may be a member of more than one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by an 'o' in the circle. Example: A Person can simultaneously be an Alumnus and an Employee of a university. Aggregation in E-R modelling

Definition Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set. When is it required? The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships. Aggregation is required when a relationship between two entities needs to participate in another relationship with a third entity. Example Consider Employee working on a Project . This forms the relationship Works_On . If we want to record the Manager who oversees this specific (Employee-Project) assignment, we aggregate Works_On into a single entity, and create a new relationship Manages between it and Manager . Mapping cardinality

Definition Mapping cardinality (or cardinality ratio) expresses the number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set. Types One-to-One (1:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B, and vice versa. One-to-Many (1:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B. An entity in B is associated with at most one entity in A. Many-to-One (N:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B. An entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A. Many-to-Many (M:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and vice versa. Functional dependency

Definition A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation. If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B. Importance Functional dependencies are the theoretical bedrock of Normalization . They are used to specify constraints on data, discover candidate keys, and decompose relations to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies. Insertion, deletion and update anomalies

The Three Anomalies Update Anomaly: If data is stored redundantly, changing it in one row requires changing it in all rows. Missing one causes inconsistency (e.g., changing a department's location). Insertion Anomaly: The inability to add data to the database due to absence of other data (e.g., unable to add a new Department because it has no Employees yet, and Employee_ID is the primary key). Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information). How Normalization Helps Normalization resolves these by decomposing large, poorly structured tables into smaller, well-structured tables where each table represents a single logical theme or entity. By linking them with foreign keys, redundancy is eliminated, which inherently solves update, insertion, and deletion anomalies. Normalization

Definition Normalization is the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy and eliminate anomalies by dividing larger tables into smaller tables and defining relationships between them using functional dependencies. The Normal Forms First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell. Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z). BCNF

Definition Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key. It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF. Difference from 3NF 3NF allows a dependency X → Y where X is NOT a super key, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF does not allow this exception. A table can be in 3NF but fail BCNF if it has overlapping candidate keys. Example Consider Relation(Student, Course, Instructor) . Keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). FD: Instructor → Course . It is in 3NF because Course is a prime attribute. However, it violates BCNF because Instructor is not a super key. Write a short note on 4NF and 5NF,

Fourth Normal Form (4NF) Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD) . A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third). Example: An Employee has multiple Skills and multiple Dependents. Storing them in one table creates massive redundancy. We split into (Emp, Skill) and (Emp, Dependent) . Fifth Normal Form (5NF) Deals with Join Dependencies . Also known as Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF). A table is in 5NF if it is in 4NF and cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data (lossless join). It ensures that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys. Lossless-join decomposition

Definition Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or extra spurious rows (creation of invalid data). Condition The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2. (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 OR R1 ∩ R2 → R2). Example Splitting Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Dept_Location) into Emp(ID, Name, Dept) and Department(Dept, Dept_Location) is lossless because their intersection, Dept , is a primary key for the Department table. Dependency-preserving decomposition and give a suitable example

Definition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation. This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together. Example Original Relation: R(A, B, C) Functional Dependencies (FDs): A → B, B → C Decomposition: R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). FDs in R1: A → B. FDs in R2: B → C. Since (A → B) ∪ (B → C) covers all original FDs, it is a dependency-preserving decomposition . Candidate Keys {A, B} + = {A, B, C, D} {B, C} + = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A) {B, D} + = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C) The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD . Generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model

Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics. Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp . Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle . Aggregation Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships. Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity. Decomposition Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.

Lossless-Join Decomposition A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples. Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 ). Dependency-Preserving Decomposition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together. How is decomposition related to normalization Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form.

Example Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName . This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency ( EmpID → DeptID → DeptName ). Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy: 1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID) 2. Department(DeptID, DeptName) This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving. Table-level constraints are defined at the end of the table creation and can span multiple columns. A table-level constraint is compulsory when defining a composite key (a constraint that involves more than one column). Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), keeping Dept_ID as the primary key CREATE TABLE Department ( Dept_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Dept_Name VARCHAR(50) ); Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Dept_ID, Salary), where Emp_ID is the primary key, Name cannot be left blank and Email must be unique CREATE TABLE Employee ( Emp_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE, Dept_ID INT, Salary DECIMAL(10,2) ); Using ALTER TABLE, add a foreign key on Employee ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID); Using ALTER TABLE, put a check constraint on the Employee table so that Salary is always greater than zero ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (Salary > 0); Table can have more than one UNIQUE constraint but only one PRIMARY KEY A Primary Key is strictly designed to

be the single, definitive row identifier used by the database engine to organize and index the physical storage (e.g. clustered index). There can only be one physical ordering. However, multiple columns may have naturally unique data (like an Email or Phone number), which is why multiple UNIQUE constraints are permitted to enforce business rules. Numeric functions ROUND, TRUNCATE, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT, giving an example of each ROUND(n, d) : Rounds n to d decimal places. ROUND(3.456, 2) → 3.46 TRUNCATE(n, d) : Cuts off n at d decimal places without rounding. TRUNCATE(3.456, 2) → 3.45 CEIL(n) : Returns the smallest integer ≥ n . CEIL(3.14) → 4 FLOOR(n) : Returns the largest integer ≤ n . FLOOR(3.8) → 3 ABS(n) : Returns the absolute (positive) value. ABS(-5) → 5 MOD(x, y) : Returns the remainder of x/y. MOD(10, 3) → 1 POWER(x, y) : Returns x raised to power y. POWER(2, 3) → 8 SQRT(n) : Returns the square root. SQRT(16) → 4 Round off 78 SELECT ROUND(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.35 SELECT TRUNCATE(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.34 Reason : ROUND evaluates the third decimal digit (5) and mathematically rounds up. TRUNCATE simply drops all digits

after the 2nd decimal place without any mathematical evaluation. Write a query on PRODUCT_MAST to display each Product_Name along SELECT Product_Name, ROUND(Price, 0) AS Rounded_Price FROM PRODUCT_MAST; Find the remainder when 29 is divided by 4 -- Find remainder SELECT MOD(29, 4); -- Check if odd/even (if remainder is 1, it is odd) SELECT MOD(29, 2); Find the square of 12 SELECT POWER(12, 2) AS Square, SQRT(144) AS Root; Date functions CURDATE, DATEDIFF, DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB and DATE_FORMAT, giving an example of each CURDATE() : Returns the current system date. Ex: SELECT CURDATE(); DATEDIFF(date1, date2) : Returns the number of days between two dates. Ex: SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-10-10', '2023-10-01'); → 9 DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL expr unit) : Adds a time interval to a date. Ex: SELECT DATE_ADD('2023-01-01', INTERVAL 5 DAY); DATE_FORMAT(date, format) : Formats a date string. Ex: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CURDATE(), '%Y-%m-%d'); String functions CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTRING and TRIM/REPLACE, giving an example of each CONCAT(s1, s2) : Joins two or more strings. Ex: CONCAT('Data', 'base') → 'Database' UPPER(s) / LOWER(s) : Converts a string to all uppercase or lowercase. Ex: UPPER('sql') → 'SQL' LENGTH(s) : Returns the number of characters in a string. Ex: LENGTH('DBMS') → 4 SUBSTRING(s, start, len) : Extracts a part

of a string. Ex: SUBSTRING('Database', 1, 4) → 'Data' TRIM(s) : Removes leading and trailing spaces. Ex: TRIM(' SQL ') → 'SQL' REPLACE(s, old, new) : Replaces all occurrences of a substring. Ex: REPLACE('DBMS', 'M', 'B') → 'DBBS' Using DATEDIFF, find the number of days between '2023-01-01' and '2023-12-31' SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-12-31', '2023-01-01') AS Days_Difference; (Note: Syntax may vary slightly by DBMS. In MySQL, it returns 364.) Using DATE_ADD, add 45 days to the date '2024-02-01' SELECT DATE_ADD('2024-02-01', INTERVAL 45 DAY) AS New_Date; Write a query to extract only the year and month from the date '2025-03-22' SELECT YEAR('2025-03-22') AS Year, MONTH('2025-03-22') AS Month; Alternatively, using DATE_FORMAT in MySQL: SELECT DATE_FORMAT('2025-03-22', '%Y-%m'); Write a query on the STUDENT table that displays the full name of every student by joining First_Name and Last_Name SELECT CONCAT(First_Name, ' ', Last_Name) AS Full_Name FROM STUDENT; Find the length of the string 'Normalization', and separately extract its first six characters SELECT LENGTH('Normalization') AS Str_Length, SUBSTRING('Normalization', 1, 6) AS Extracted_Str; UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and MINUS/EXCEPT Set Operators: UNION : Combines results of two queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL : Combines results of two queries, keeping all duplicates. INTERSECT : Returns only the rows that appear in

both queries. MINUS / EXCEPT : Returns rows from the first query that are not present in the second. Condition for application (Union Compatibility): Both SELECT statements must have the same number of columns. The corresponding columns must have compatible data types in the same order. Write a query to list every student who is a member of CLUB_CODING or CLUB_MUSIC or both, SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING UNION SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Write a query that lists all the rows of CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC together without removing duplicate names SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING UNION ALL SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Write a query to find students who are members of both CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING INTERSECT SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Write a query to find students who are in CLUB_CODING but not in CLUB_MUSIC SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING EXCEPT -- (or MINUS in Oracle) SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Yes, the order matters. A EXCEPT B returns elements in A that are not in B. B EXCEPT A would return students in CLUB_MUSIC who are not in CLUB_CODING. Transaction A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely

or not at all. ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B): Atomicity : "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. Consistency : The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction. Isolation : Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway. Durability : Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes. Transaction State Diagram COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT COMMIT : Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently. ROLLBACK : Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit. SAVEPOINT : Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101'; SAVEPOINT step1; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; -- If something goes

wrong here: ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update COMMIT; -- Saves the final state Write a transaction that transfers Rs START TRANSACTION; SAVEPOINT before_transfer; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A103'; COMMIT; Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, CASE WHEN Balance >= 25000 THEN 'High' WHEN Balance >= 15000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS Balance_Category FROM ACCOUNT; Write a query SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, IF(Balance < 15000, 'Low Balance Alert', 'OK') AS Status FROM ACCOUNT; Write a query SELECT Acc_No, Name, COALESCE(Nominee_Name, 'Not Registered') AS Nominee FROM ACCOUNT; In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger Stored Procedure : A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine. Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT) : Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys. Cursor : A database object used to

retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure. Trigger : A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table. BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables). NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted). Purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing. DECLARE ... HANDLER : Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION ). SIGNAL : Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
